articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration push to set aside thousands of California ballots
articles.description: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration push to set aside thousands of California ballots AP News Supreme court rules against Trump over bid to force California to set aside ballots The Guardian Ninth Circuit wipes out ruling allowing Trump administration to threaten election officials Democracy Docket Judge Declines to Halt D.H.S. Demands for States to Screen Ballots The New York Times Supreme Court rejects DOJ's
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration’s push to force California to set aside thousands of ballots from people the federal government claims are noncitizens, a decision that came hours before the final day of voting in the pivotal midterm elections. ▶ Follow live updates on the midterm elections The high court refused to immediately intervene in a case involving 20,000 people the Republican administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the largely Democratic state’s voter rolls. The swift rejection capped a string of losses for the president’s effort to intervene in the election before the counting of ballots to decide who controls Congress in the last two years of his second term. No justices publicly dissented. “The Court rejected Trump’s emergency request without even asking the other side to respond,” California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, posted on X. “Democracy won.” Several lower courts also rejected the Justice Department’s push to set aside the challenged California ballots until the voters’ citizenship status could be verified. And in a case that revolved around the future certification of Alaska’s election results, a judge did not even hold a hearing before dismissing a Trump-ordered suit to prevent a possible Democratic Senate win. The high court did not detail its reasoning in the California ballot case, as is common in emergency decisions. The justices previously rejected Trump’s push to restrict mail ballots around the country in September, even though the justices have sided with his administration in a series of other emergency docket appeals. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, also a Democrat, noted the administration’s legal losing streak in a statement. “Courts have now rejected the Trump Administration’s attempts to interfere in California’s elections not once, not twice, not three times, but four times — from the district court to the Ninth Circuit to the U.S. Supreme Court,” Bonta said. “This latest decision should put an end to the Administration’s attempt to disrupt California’s elections through emergency court orders.” The Republican administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite it being a rare problem. California officials said the administration’s list appeared to be filled with errors and said setting the ballots aside could effectively disenfranchise legal voters. Also on Monday in Washington, another federal judge ruled against the administration’s efforts to make last-minute demands of California election officials, finding they violated the U.S. Constitution. “The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution’s Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone,” Chief Judge James Boasberg wrote. Later Monday, ruling in a separate case, Boasberg declined to issue yet another order that the administration cease its demands. He ruled that Democratic groups that sued did not have legal standing and that the issue already had been dealt with by states and the courts. The administration, for its part, said segregating the ballots was a modest request that would eventually allow legal votes to still be counted. Its push has faced not only the remarkable series of losses in court, but criticism for waiting until a few weeks before the election to make its demands of California election officials with a list that even the Department of Justice admits is not entirely reliable. During a hearing over whether to lift her order forbidding the administration from threatening to prosecute election workers who let potentially illegal voters cast ballots, U.S. District Court Judge Trina Thompson drilled down on reports of widespread inaccuracies in the Justice Department’s data. “Would you agree there’s a high error rate?” the San Francisco-based judge asked Kenneth Kao, a Justice Department attorney. “That’s a fair statement,” Kao said. “That’s why we ask for the registrars’ aid in verifying these are all valid voters.” At the same time, Bill Essayli, the federal prosecutor running the Justice Department’s Los Angeles office, said at a news conference he was highly confident the people on the list were not entitled to vote. “This isn’t speculation. This isn’t a theory,” Essayli said, later conceding there may be errors on the list. Rather than lift her order, Thompson late Monday expanded it to require the Department of Justice to inform her ahead of time of any criminal investigations or prosecutions involving its noncitizen list. Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. Each of the state’s roughly 23 million registered voters is mailed a ballot, and more than 6 million have already been returned, according to Associated Press elections data. “The DOJ’s baseless challenge was yet another attempt at federal overreach and voter suppression,” Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel, said in a statement in reaction to the Supreme Court decision. “We will not stand for the Trump Administration’s bullying campaign, and we will continue to use every tool at our disposal to ensure the American people’s voices are not silenced.” California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible. Lower courts swiftly sided with the state, with a district judge warning last week that segregating ballots would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process. “If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat. A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favor. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California’s unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the “violation of federal law.” Associated Press writers Sophie Austin in Sacramento, California, and Safiyah Riddle in Los Angeles contributed to this report. Follow the AP’s coverage of the U.S. Supreme Court at https://apnews.com/hub/us-supreme-court.

Michigan State University trustee sues, says ethics policy is unconstitutional
articles.description: MSU's policy was updated last spring and now includes a clause requiring trustees to support board decisions, which some view as a loyalty clause.
articles.content: (EMMA WINOWIECKI / Michigan Radio)Michigan State University Trustee Mike Balow says he has worked behind the scenes for months to get the university’s board to modify its controversial ethics policy, updated last spring to include what some viewed as a loyalty clause amid some trustees publicly questioning university policies.Balow decided he’s had enough. This week, he filed a federal lawsuit against board Chair Briana Scott and board Secretary Stefan Fletcher, alleging the updated policy is unconstitutional.The updated policy is viewed by some as silencing elected officials but supporters say it reinforces board member responsibilities. It includes provisions such as one requiring trustees to support and not undermine decisions made by the majority of the board and another requiring trustees to act after board decisions “consistent with our fiduciary duties, including the duty of loyalty.”“History teaches that self-government breaks down when those in power use governmental authority to silence dissent,” says the lawsuit, filed on Balow’s behalf by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a national organization fighting for rights of those on and off college campuses.“Under the board’s new rules, trustees may praise MSU’s leadership all they want, but they face sanctions if they publicly criticize it,” the lawsuit continues. “That is blatant viewpoint discrimination, repugnant to our Constitution and political tradition.”Scott, the board chair, said MSU’s updated ethics policy contains similar provisions to one enacted for Wayne State University ’s board and state lawmakers are expected to follow the rules of their respective House and Senate chambers, as enforced by the speaker and majority leader.“The purpose of the Code of Ethics and Conduct is to help ensure the Board can effectively govern in service to students, faculty, staff, parents, research partners, taxpayers and the broader public,” Scott said in a statement. “The code does not limit speech or restrict members of governing boards from raising concerns, providing oversight or questioning decisions; instead, it establishes good and commonsense governance practices.”Balow’s lawsuit is the second filed this month against MSU officials by a board member. Trustee Rema Vassar last week filed a federal lawsuit against MSU President Kevin Guskiewicz and others, alleging racial discrimination.“The university will respond to the accusations in Trustee Vassar’s lawsuit through the applicable legal process,” MSU spokesperson Amber McCann said.Balow said that he and Vassar have been shut out of about 20 MSU events where other trustees were invited since they decided not to sign the policy in May. And the events from which they have been excluded go beyond football games, Balow added, from the Mackinac Policy Conference to the president’s State of the University address to a dinner to thank employers who worked to restore power to campus after a major outage.Even when he tried to address it on a board phone call, he said the response from other trustees was “crickets” and then they moved on.“We are going to take a deep dive into the constitutionality of the code and we are going to show it is not the right policy for MSU or any university that silences board members,” said Balow. “We are going to make Michigan State a better place.”___This story was originally published by Bridge Michigan and distributed through a partnership with The Associated Press.

articles.title: Powerful Haitian gang leader writes UN seeking dialogue as clashes intensify
articles.content: SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — One of Haiti’s most powerful gang leaders confirmed to The Associated Press on Monday that he wrote the U.N. Secretary General and requested that the organization send a delegation to Haiti for dialogue and mediation amid fears that Salvadoran troops deployed after the disappearance of four aviation technicians from that country could escalate violence. Wilson Joseph, best known as Lanmò Sanjou and leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, told the AP in his first interview with a major international media company that the technicians are dead and that the Oct. 18 attack occurred while they were in the territory of Chen Mechan, another gang. He did not provide evidence; Haiti’s government has said the four Salvadorans were abducted, and the Salvadoran government believes they are alive. Joseph said he is upset that drone attacks are killing civilians in the area, with clashes intensifying ever since a U.N.-backed gang-suppression force working with Haitian police and soldiers, as well as Vectus Global — the private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL and Blackwater founder Erik Prince — began fighting armed men in Plaine du Cul-de-Sac near Port-au-Prince following the attack on the Salvadorans. Joseph said that the same Haitian politicians who armed gangs in Haiti are bringing foreign troops “to destroy us.” He said he had a message for El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, who recently deployed 2,000 troops to Haiti: “The Haitian politicians are the father of the gangs and the rebels. ... The politicians don’t want this to stop.” In his letter, Joseph wrote: “Given Mr. Nayib Bukele’s vengeful remarks, expectations, and threats, I fear this situation will lead to an escalation of violence and a logic of reprisals, of which the Haitian people would be the first victims.” Joseph alleged in his interview with the AP that politicians are warning him about any security operations headed his way. He added that he doesn’t have a problem with forces arresting gang members, but he accused forces of dropping drones and killing children and the elderly. Joseph said he’s ready to have a dialogue and lay down guns, although when asked what he wanted in exchange, he declined to say, adding he would talk about that when he sits down with a peace commission. He also rejected accusations that 400 Mawozo has killed innocent Haitians. In a statement late Monday, U.N. spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said they had received a letter with Joseph’s signature: “However, receipt of such a letter does not constitute endorsement of its contents, recognition of its author, or a position by the United Nations.” He noted that the vast majority of Salvadoran military personnel are not deployed under the U.N.-backed gang suppression force, “and therefore fall outside” the U.N. mandate and reporting. “We want to underscore that the United Nations remains concerned that communities continue to bear the brunt of the situation in Haiti,” he said, adding that any type of security operation “must be carried out in full accordance with applicable international law.” Joseph asserted in his letter that recent events in Plaine du Cul-de-Sac, especially where another gang, Chen Mechan, operates, “are causing serious concern.” Joseph wrote that he was “officially available” to receive the delegation that he “respectfully” requested and would “participate in any meeting aimed at finding a peaceful solution, a dialogue agreement and a sustainable stabilization process.” “I remain convinced that dialogue must prevail over force,” he said. “The protection of civilians, particularly children and vulnerable families, must be at the heart of any international initiative,” Joseph wrote. More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured across Haiti from January to mid-September, according to the U.N. In the two-page letter sent Nov. 1, Joseph said he has “officially raised the white flag” since Aug. 20 and seeks a “peaceful solution to the national crisis, in particular through the opening of a dialogue between the international forces present in Haiti and the 400 Mawozo group.” The group, which roughly translates to “400 Simpletons,” operates largely in Croix-des-Bouquets, a community near Port-au-Prince. A spokesperson for the gang who declined to be identified accused the government of abandoning that area and asserted that’s why Joseph took charge of it. The gang is known for carrying out kidnappings, including those in October 2021 of 17 missionaries, 16 of them from the U.S. and one from Canada. There were five children in that group, and all were eventually released. The spokesperson denied they were kidnappings but rather a “justice” measure given sexual abuse charges against a former missionary. The spokesperson also said that 400 Mawozo is not a terrorist organization, and that young people lacking education who are allegedly being used by politicians are being killed. The U.S. government has issued a $1 million reward for Joseph, who was indicted in the U.S. in 2022 on charges of hostage taking and conspiracy to commit hostage taking.

articles.title: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
articles.description: Y Combinator Garry Tan has jokingly admitted that he's suffered from "cyber psychosis” and barely sleeps sometimes because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast, The Builders, Tan put a price tag on his passion.
articles.content: Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders, set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion. “I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said. On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life. “It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said. He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.” As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said. For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.” Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down. “It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.” But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. articles.title: LGBTQ Michiganders feel betrayed as Haley Stevens ditches Abdul El-Sayed. What you need to know.
articles.description: This story was originally published by Uncloseted Media. On June 5, Democratic Michigan state representative and then-Senate hopeful Haley Stevens posted to Facebook that “Mike Rogers’ record on LGBTQ+ rights is repulsive. He has no business representing Michiganders.” Fast forward to Sunday: Stevens sent shockwaves across the country when she endorsed Rogers at a press […]
articles.content: U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) presented local business owner James Cristbrook of Shain Park Realtors with a new Pride flag to replace the Pride flag insignia that had been stolen from his business’s window twice in 2023. | Stevens office photo This story was originally published by Uncloseted Media. On June 5, Democratic Michigan state representative and then-Senate hopeful Haley Stevens posted to Facebook that “Mike Rogers’ record on LGBTQ+ rights is repulsive. He has no business representing Michiganders.” Fast forward to Sunday: Stevens sent shockwaves across the country when she endorsed Rogers at a press conference in front of Perfecting Church in Detroit. “When you see hate, when you see us standing with Hasan Piker and repeated hate, it’s not acceptable,” she said, referring to the progressive Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and his connection to the controversial left-wing streamer. While the endorsement was described by news outlets as a bombshell, tensions were already mounting between her and El-Sayed, to whom she lost the Democratic primary in August. Stevens was slated to appear at a rally for El-Sayed’s campaign on Sunday, but announced beforehand that she would only go if he agreed to condemn a political ad by a PAC that links U.S. support for Israel’s war in Gaza to increased costs of living domestically. El-Sayed criticized her for this, stating that she “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago,” and later adding that he does not agree with the ad’s contents. This came after months of heated disagreement between the two over Israel, with El-Sayed calling the country’s assault on Gaza a “genocide” and Stevens calling it a “strong ally of the United States of America.” Stevens’ endorsement received immediate backlash: Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer called it a “despicable betrayal,” former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi wrote that she has betrayed Michigan families, and Michigan’s Democratic Party chair announced that she “is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.” While Stevens said her decision was “personal and private,” critics questioned why she made the announcement at a press conference in front of a Black church, amidst attempts by Rogers’ campaign to win over Black Michiganders. She finished her remarks by saying, “It’s gonna be a close election and everyone can take a look at the facts.” Uncloseted Media decided to do just that to understand if Stevens’ decision to vote for Rogers over El-Sayed lines up with combatting hate. Here’s what you need to know: Mike Rogers’ Track Record on LGBTQ Issues While Stevens has emphasized that her opposition to El-Sayed is rooted in opposing hate, Rogers has a sordid record on LGBTQ issues. During his tenure in the U.S. House of Representatives, Rogers voted against cornerstone LGBTQ rights legislation including the Employment Non-Discrimination Act, the repeal of “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell” and the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act, which expanded the federal definition of hate crimes to include those motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity. He has called being gay a “lifestyle choice” and voted multiple times in favor of a constitutional amendment banning gay marriage. Rogers is also a staunch supporter of President Donald Trump, whose administration has waged an all-out attack on the LGBTQ community by slashing crucial health and support programs, pressuring states to exclude trans people from most aspects of life and erasing information about the community’s history. “Haley Stevens just does not give a fuck about queer people,” Cat Hadley, a progressive campaign strategist and Ann Arbor District Library Board trustee, told Uncloseted Media. “No one who genuinely cared about queer people would ever do this. And frankly, unfortunately, it’s not surprising to see an elected official throw an entire community under the bus for any political gain.” Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers speaking at a press conference in Sterling Heights, Mich., as he rolls out a new affordable housing finance and regulation busting policy. Feb. 10, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance Rogers and Islamophobia Rogers has also levied Islamophobic attacks against El-Sayed. At a debate in October, he referenced Al-Qaeda, the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas and Hezbollah in an attempt to associate El-Sayed’s campaign with terrorism. Rogers has also stood by Trump’s racist attacks on El-Sayed throughout the race. At a rally in Michigan last month, Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist,” said he “wants [America] to go to Sharia law” and that “he would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.” “If Abdul and the Democrats win, they will open the floodgates and invite hordes of jihadists to our shores, creating a nightmare of violence and terror until you cannot even have a Christmas,” Trump told the crowd. Rather than debunking the false and racist claims, Rogers attended the rally and took the stage with the president. When asked by NBC News if he agreed with comments from Trump, he said, “I don’t understand the national press. They have to work and twist themselves in knots not to understand Abdul’s relationship with the thinking of the Muslim Brotherhood.” El-Sayed’s Track Record on LGBTQ Issues El-Sayed, by contrast, has championed LGBTQ issues, vowing to be “a lion for rights” if elected and supporting gender-affirming care for minors, anti-discrimination protections and the undoing of HIV criminalization laws. As a health director, he ran Michigan’s largest Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program and collaborated with a local LGBTQ nonprofit to train staffers in the department on LGBTQ inclusivity. “I am deeply disappointed by Congresswoman Stevens’ actions,” Joanna Whaley, a trans woman running for state representative in Michigan, told Uncloseted Media in a text message. “Abdul El-Sayed has continually pushed a message of inclusion and unity across our state while the Rogers campaign has run the most racist homophobic campaign I have ever seen in Michigan politics.” Abdul El-Sayed, Democratic U.S. Senate nominee (left) and Abbas Alawieh, Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 2nd Senate District (left), at a “Hate Has No Home in Michigan” event at Christ Episcopal & Mother of the Savior Church in Dearborn to address “the recent rise in hateful rhetoric targeting Michigan communities,” on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan Advance) The Use of Black Communities as ‘Political Props’ Some Michiganders have also taken umbrage with Stevens’ decision to appear with Rogers at a Black church after making the endorsement. DeNiro Jones, an LGBTQ public policy strategist from Detroit who has worked with Democratic candidates, told Uncloseted Media that it “raises a serious concern about using Black communities as political props.” “Too often, Black voters are treated as an audience to be managed rather than a constituency to be respected,” Jones wrote in a text message. “We understand the stakes for our communities, and we deserve to be engaged on the substance, not used as a backdrop.” “Stevens herself described Rogers’ record on LGBTQ rights as ‘repulsive.’ That record does not disappear because she has changed her endorsement,” he says. “Political disagreements do not erase the consequences of public policy, and Black voters should never be expected to lend credibility to a decision simply because it was presented at one of our churches.” The Reaction All of this has contributed to widespread condemnation of Stevens’ endorsement. Several of Haley Stevens’ staffers resigned in protest of her endorsement of Rogers, with her longtime chief of staff writing that they were “shocked and heartbroken” by the decision. Shannon Watts, the founder of a pro-gun control nonprofit who endorsed Stevens in the primary, called the move “pathetic” and asked how “Haley Stevens is ‘condemning hate’ by endorsing someone hateful?” And gay Democratic congressional candidate Jeremy Moss, who has not endorsed El-Sayed and publicly disagrees with his stances on Israel, released a statement saying, “Openly cheerleading Mike Rogers is unacceptable. … Rogers, with his abysmal anti-LGBTQ record, would gleefully confirm Supreme Court justices who will rollback the rights that I have fought hard to protect.” Other LGBTQ lawmakers in the state have also come out against the endorsement, including State Reps. Laurie Pohutsky and Jason Morgan as well as former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who told CNN, “I don’t know what she’s thinking.” Additional reporting by Spencer Macnaughton.

ICC president hits back at Trump administration penalties in remote UN address
articles.description: ICC president hits back at Trump administration penalties in remote UN address AP News ICC president accuses Trump administration of trying to obstruct international justice The Hill Threats to the Global Rule of Law: A Warning from the ICC President Nippon.com How Europe Is Defying Trump by Rallying Around the ICC Time Magazine ICC president urges U.N. members to defend court against U.S. sanctions The Japan Times
articles.content: UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The president of the International Criminal Court accused the Trump administration of trying to obstruct international justice by imposing penalties on the tribunal and vowed that it would not succeed. Judge Tomoko Akane of Japan, briefing the United Nations remotely on Monday because of U.S. sanctions, called on all 193 U.N. member nations — not just the 125 countries that are part of the ICC — “to take concrete action, individually and collectively, in defense of the court.” President Donald Trump’s administration has imposed a series of sanctions on ICC officials and then targeted the entire court last month as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel. Akane said her remote address to the U.N. General Assembly was a result of the “extraordinary” and “unprecedented” U.S. steps threatening judges, prosecutors and the ICC itself as an institution. She stressed the timing of the Trump administration announcing sweeping new sanctions on the court on Oct. 9. That was the day the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African jurist Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge, for her efforts to promote peace and international law. “The contrast could not be starker,” the ICC president said. “On the one hand, global recognition of the value of international justice, on the other, an attempt to subdue the institution that embodies it.” The ICC was set up in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide when countries are unwilling or unable to do so. The United States is not a party to the court. The State Department had no immediate comment on Akane’s remarks. In announcing the latest sanctions, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. “will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us.” The ICC president countered Monday by saying, “Let me be clear: The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes.” The European Union and other supporters stepped to the podium at the U.N. General Assembly to strongly support the ICC and its work seeking justice for humanity’s worst crimes.

articles.title: It’s Hard to Be ________ Right Now
articles.description: Jewish and Muslim residents are increasingly being asked to denounce actions they had nothing to do with.
articles.content: Political leaders, religious officials and private citizens are increasingly being asked to denounce the actions of others. Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed — who would become the nation’s first Muslim senator — has been pressured by opponents and allies alike to denounce antisemitism. Yet, El-Sayed has also been the target of anti-Muslim rhetoric throughout the campaign, including President Donald Trump saying El-Sayed was “on the side of the terrorists” at a recent Port Huron campaign event, according to NPR. At the same time, American Jews feel under attack, and some feel pressured to denounce the actions of the Israeli government amid accusations of state-sanctioned genocide against Palestinians following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas terrorist attack and kidnapping of Israeli citizens. East Lansing Info spoke with local leaders of both faith communities to learn more about the challenges and frustrations they and their congregations are experiencing. “What we have seen is a fundamental reassessing of what it means to be a Jew in America, or a Jew in any country, frankly, at this time,” said Rabbi Matthew Kaufman of Lansing’s Congregation Kehillat Israel. “And it’s a less comfortable assessment than it ever used to be. I would say that one thing that has changed – and this would probably apply more to secular Jews – Jews who didn’t have any particular affiliation before, who may not have actually prioritized a Jewish community, or Jewish observance, or Jewish living particularly in any way, suddenly had their awareness – their feelings – jarred into awakening around Jewish identity. And so Jewish identity became more important and more central to figure out for people who had never particularly thought about it before.” Kaufman, an Okemos native who grew up in the congregation he now leads, said things feel less safe and stable for Jews, leaving many questioning their safety, security and place in society. Jewish organizations in the Greater Lansing area have faced numerous acts of vandalism and threats in recent years. Just last year, someone threw rocks at and spray-painted Nazi symbols on the MSU Chabad Jewish Center in East Lansing. Protests across U.S. college campuses have also caused tension for Jewish students, Kaufman said. “It was far more intense in other cities and in other campuses than it was locally,” he said, “and that doesn’t mean it was not present locally, but we did not experience the same intensity here as we’ve seen elsewhere. That said, it hasn’t been absent of tension. So what I’ve noticed is that for Jewish students at Michigan State there’s a lot more cautiousness about publicly connecting to Jewish identity.” Kaufman said the contention has created two categories in the eyes of some: “good Jews,” who disavow any connection to Zionism, and “bad Jews,” who do not. Some Jews have felt compelled to accept that distinction, he said, while others have no problem with it. But Kaufman said the vast majority of American Jews believe Israel has a right to exist. For Muslims, the pressure to answer for the actions and beliefs of others is a familiar experience. Islamic Center of East Lansing Imam Sohail Chaudhry, said Islamophobia has repeatedly resurfaced throughout his life, particularly during moments of political upheaval. “It keeps coming back,” he said. “I remember what happened after 9/11. I was a student back then. It’s the same thing which keeps resurfacing. In the first Trump election in 2016, the same thing happened. This idea that Muslims are the enemy and demonizing the Muslim community, and portraying them as people who [are] trying to take over America, and misconceptions around terms like Sharia law and jihad and women’s rights in Islam. It’s the same Islamophobia which keeps coming back after every few years, whenever the politicians see the need.” Chaudhry has served the Greater Lansing Islamic community for nearly 12 years, relocating here after 15 years in West Virginia. He said many Americans do not know what the Muslim Brotherhood is or what connection, if any, it has to Muslims in the United States. Still, El-Sayed’s opponents have tried to draw ties between him and the group, a connection fact checkers say lacks evidence. Older worshippers, however, recognize what Chaudhry described as an organized, multimillion-dollar Islamophobia industry that spends money employing people who hate Islam. While older generations of Muslims have experienced these cycles before, Chaudhry said younger Muslims are confronting them for the first time. “Many of them are confused,” he said. “They don’t know what’s going on.” And for both religious leaders, the impact on young people is among their greatest concerns. “The biggest challenge more recently for a lot of Muslim youth,” Chaudhry said, “is going to school and being identified as Muslims and the bullying that goes on. The subtle forms of Islamophobia that many students witness.” He said young Muslims encounter hateful messages on social media, leaving them confused and under pressure. Many turn to him for counseling. Chaudhry said one of the biggest challenges facing his community is maintaining a Muslim identity, particularly for those whose faith is outwardly visible, including women who wear the hijab, men who wear beards and anyone who prays in public. Kaufman expressed similar concerns about the messages children in his congregation encounter in public schools, saying some of the narratives they hear about their faith and identity can be harmful to their development. “When we talk to everybody about Israel,” he said, “are we really only going to talk about the government? What about the culture? What about our connection? What about the values we share and the peoplehood? What about the complexity of life there?” Kaufman said the synagogue teaches children Hebrew to help them develop positive connections to their Jewish identity, giving them strength as they grow. He believes Jewish communities need to do a better job responding to hostility and equipping their children with an understanding of Jewish history and identity, “so they can have some kind of defenses against the narratives that they’re hearing, which are … in fact, just lies being told about Jews. “And it hammers at you, you know, if you’re a person who’s being told, and especially for young people, you know, you’re being told you should be ashamed of yourself — and if you don’t have the defenses to say, ‘Well, actually, the story of the Jewish people returning to the land of Israel, our historic land, is a miracle story, and it’s a wonderful source of pride,’” Kaufman said. Beyond concerns about young people, both religious leaders described the burden of being held responsible for actions committed by others who share their faith or identity. For Kaufman, that burden has become particularly pronounced amid criticism of Israel’s military actions. He offered a historical comparison, invoking the antisemitic accusation known as “blood libel” where Jewish people have been falsely and baselessly accused of murdering non-Jewish children to use their blood in religious rituals. Kaufman recounted the story of Simon of Trent, a 15th century Christian boy whose death was blamed on Jews accused of using his blood in a religious observance. “I can’t even wrap my mind around it, it’s so warped,” Kaufman said, pausing his story. Kaufman said the accusation expanded beyond those initially blamed, creating a belief that Jews collectively bore responsibility for the boy’s death. “It is a blood libel,” he said. “The impact of it is, now, if you do not disavow this ‘genocidal state,’ you’re complicit. So now you’re partaking of the blame. You see, now you can become part of the accused group.” Kaufman pointed to several acts of violence as examples of the dangers facing Jewish communities and individuals, including the firebombing of Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s home during Passover, the murder of an elderly woman in Colorado who was calling for Hamas to release Israeli hostages and a truck that was driven into a West Bloomfield synagogue while children were eating snacks inside. “And so what is very scary for Jewish communities is not only that expansion, but the normalization of what this rhetoric means,” he said. “If there is a kind of acceptance that the normalization of the various negative ways in which Israel and its government are referred to, if there’s a normalization of this as a generalizable accusation, then Jews risk being considered complicit in any of the things of which the state of Israel is being accused. It ends up not being a confined political issue of foreign policy. It’s something that becomes very real to lived Jewish life in areas that have absolutely nothing to do with Israel.” Chaudhry said Muslims understand the experience of being blamed collectively for the actions of a few. “This is a problem across the different religions, is that events of a few have to be answered by the whole,” he said. “And of course, they do not represent us. There have been, in the past, many times where things happen elsewhere in the world, and the Muslim community is blamed for it, and we are questioned about it, and I’m sure the Jewish community also feels in a similar place.” For Chaudhry, education and understanding are essential to breaking that cycle. He emphasized the importance of learning about the religions and cultures of others rather than relying on portrayals offered by politicians or the media. “Then we find out how many commonalities and similarities there are, and how all the faiths in the world agree when it comes to so many of the human rights and standing up for justice and taking care of the poor and the needy and the refugees,” Chaudhry said. “There’s so many values that we share across different people and their beliefs. So it’s very important that we educate.” Chaudhry said people need to learn about Islam beyond how it is portrayed in public discourse. He added that Muslims have a responsibility to learn about other faiths and belief systems, too. Neither Kaufman nor Chaudhry pretended that their religious communities agree on every issue. Chaudhry acknowledged the complicated history between the faiths and said their leaders may differ on many fronts. But they work to ensure those differences do not destroy their local relationships. Both men spoke of the ways local leaders from different faith communities have shown up for one another, even amid disagreements and tensions elsewhere. The Interfaith Clergy Association of Greater Lansing organized a special service of healing and unity after the Oct. 7, 2023 attack, collecting donations for local synagogues and the mosque to support increased security efforts. “It was really this incredible coming together of these various faith communities,” Kaufman said, “and…the Imam and I focused on getting the message out there that we care about our neighbors and ourselves right here. Never mind what is going on in America around us, and never mind what is going on overseas. Our priority is our neighbors and our friends here, and we need to look out for each other.” Chaudhry said the faith communities will continue to work together, focusing on the shared space they inhabit and the people they can help. “At the end of the day we have to recognize that we will be leaving our children, the next generations here together, and if we want a better future for them, we cannot afford those generations to be hating each other and fighting,” he said. “Rather, we would want them to live in peace and harmony. “But it’s the people-to-people interaction that is going to change things.” Do you have a question that you would like ELi to investigate? articles.title: US Supreme Court rejects Trump DOJ’s attempt to freeze California vote counting
articles.description: The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday, mere hours before Election Day in the midterms that will determine control of Congress, denied the Trump administration’s final attempt to force California to set aside the ballots of 20,000 people it suspects are noncitizens. The decision marked a significant blow to President Donald Trump’s bid to control voting in […]
articles.content: The U.S. Supreme Court on April 9, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday, mere hours before Election Day in the midterms that will determine control of Congress, denied the Trump administration’s final attempt to force California to set aside the ballots of 20,000 people it suspects are noncitizens. The decision marked a significant blow to President Donald Trump’s bid to control voting in the country’s most populous state and capped a whirlwind three weeks of legal war between the U.S. Department of Justice and California’s state and local election officials. The Supreme Court’s denial also removed the possibility of a last-minute ruling that could have led to chaos if officials were forced to scramble to follow the Justice Department’s demands. The court denied the Justice Department’s request late Monday afternoon in a one-sentence order. It noted no dissents, and offered no reasoning, as is often the case in decisions on emergency requests. The Justice Department had demanded that election officials set aside the ballots of about 20,000 people on a list developed by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. The DOJ told election officials the ballots shouldn’t be tabulated unless the citizenship of the individuals could be verified. At the same time, Justice Department lawyers threatened election officials with prosecution if they counted the ballots. The Trump administration argued that the officials would be aiding and abetting noncitizen voting, a misdemeanor federal crime. Election officials in Los Angeles County received grand jury subpoenas. “Today’s decision is another blow to the Trump administration’s manufactured election emergency and a major victory for local election officials and voters across the country,” Jonathan Miller, chief program officer of Public Rights Project, which represented Los Angeles County, said in a statement. States and federal government The dispute pitted the Trump administration’s claims of executive authority against California’s power to run its own elections. The U.S. Constitution assigns states the responsibility of administering elections, though Congress can override state rules. The president — and by extension the officials under him — have no unilateral power over how states run their elections. The Justice Department on Monday morning asked for an administrative stay that would have required California to begin segregating ballots of voters on the list while the Trump administration prepares a full appeal. The Supreme Court denied the DOJ’s request without seeking briefing from California and the other parties in the case. Steve Vladeck, a professor at Georgetown University Law Center and a leading expert on the Supreme Court, wrote on social media that he couldn’t remember any case in which the court denied a Justice Department application without calling for a response. “That’s an even bigger ‘go away’ than the lack of (public) dissents,” Vladeck wrote. The DOJ didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the decision. Avoids major fallout Election officials warned of grave consequences if they were ordered to separate the ballots. Aman Bhullar, an assistant Los Angeles County registrar-recorder/county clerk, wrote in a court declaration in October that the potential fallout included halting ballot counting and in-person voting. The Supreme Court generally shies away from ordering major last-minute changes to elections. While the justices have shown greater deference to states that alter their elections, they often counsel federal courts against significant 11th-hour interventions — a doctrine that’s become known as the Purcell principle. But the Trump administration had argued that because noncitizen voting is illegal under federal law, any ballot cast by a noncitizen is unlawful. “It also follows that a State may not count such an invalid ballot,” U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in his request. Stephen Richer, a legal fellow with the Cato Institute’s Robert A. Levy Center for Constitutional Studies, noted in a statement that every California voter attests to their citizenship under penalty of perjury — the same requirement in federal law. “The federal government has suspicions — not proof — that certain voters are not citizens,” Richer wrote. “California law provides a process for challenging those voters. The federal government cannot invent its own at this late hour.” List questioned The accuracy of the list also came under intense criticism from California election officials and voting rights advocates. An immigrant rights group, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, said in a court filing Saturday that an analysis by data experts found that 42% of the names weren’t found on California’s current voter file. At least 22 names on the DHS list match names of U.S. citizens compiled by the organization, the analysis found. The Justice Department said Homeland Security used a public copy of California’s voter roll to develop the list. DHS checked the list against federal records and used the Lexis Nexis research service to analyze voter information, the Trump administration said in court filings. The DOJ repeatedly argued that once a ballot is processed, it becomes impossible to identify whether a noncitizen cast it. Yet the department didn’t ask the Supreme Court to intervene until Monday morning, days after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against the set-aside request on Friday. When Sauer did file a request with the Supreme Court, he wrote that his office had been “informed” that the Trump administration identified more than 20,000 individuals “who appear to be registered as voters in California at the time the voter-roll information was received and whom the United States believes are likely to be aliens.” Sauer’s arguments were undercut by remarks made by a Justice Department lawyer hours later. During a court hearing in California on Monday over the Trump administration’s threats against election officials, Kenneth Kao, an assistant U.S. attorney, acknowledged the list contains significant errors. “Would you agree there’s a high error rate — not nominal — but a high error rate,” Judge Trina Thompson, an appointee of President Joe Biden in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, asked. “I think that’s a fair statement,” Kao replied.

articles.title: Trajectory raises $45M to make AI model training accessible to nontechnical experts
articles.description: The one-year-old startup is now valued at $300 million.
articles.content: Whether developed by OpenAI or Anthropic or built on open source alternatives, current AI models share a critical limitation: They don’t learn from their mistakes without further training. Businesses adapting these models for specialized fields, such as law and finance, typically get around this by fine-tuning general models. However, that often requires hiring internal research teams or relying on expensive consultants, commonly known as forward-deployed engineers (FDEs). Trajectory, a startup founded about a year ago by three Stanford classmates with experience at Google DeepMind and Apple, wants to automate that process, allowing AI models to learn from feedback and continuously improve at specialized tasks. The 18-person company just announced that it raised $45 million in a Series A round at a $300 million valuation, led by Sequoia, with participation from Nvidia, Bessemer Venture Partners, and Bain Capital Ventures. Trajectory co-founder Ronak Malde compared foundational models to a very smart PhD student who’s always starting a new job. “But what the economy values is someone who worked on the job for 30 years,” he told TechCrunch. The startup aims to solve this problem through an approach known as continual learning. Businesses using Trajectory can start with an open source AI model and connect the platform to their applications, allowing it to collect feedback on how the model performs. Trajectory then uses that information to retrain the model, helping it improve at specialized tasks over time. With Trajectory, lawyers, doctors, and other specialists can improve the models near automatically themselves, Malde said. That capability could make deploying specialized AI faster and cheaper. Companies like Harvey and Rogo are already using Trajectory’s platform to post-train open source models, helping them perform more like experienced lawyers or financial analysts by learning from previous tasks, such as reviewing a particular type of legal contract or valuing a company using a specific methodology. Trajectory’s other customers include Decagon, Mercor, and Nvidia. The startup is now making its post-training platform publicly available. The people using Trajectory decide “what good looks like for their organization and can turn that into improvements for their model,” Malde said. Trajectory’s approach to continual learning shares some similarities with recursive self-improvement (RSI), the idea that AI systems can improve their own capabilities. But co-founder Michael Elabd argues that keeping humans involved in the training process makes Trajectory’s approach safer, since autonomous self-improvement could lead to unintended or even dangerous outcomes. Trajectory isn’t the only startup trying to automate post-training. Other companies going after this market include Thinking Machines Lab, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati and the company behind the fine-tuning platform Tinker, Applied Compute, which was valued at $3.25 billion last month, and Prime Intellect, a platform that helps companies build and train their own AI agents. Malde believes the startup’s biggest advantage is its team. He was among the handful of researchers Google DeepMind acqui-hired from Windsurf. Elabd also worked at DeepMind, while Trajectory’s third co-founder, Arjun Karanam, previously worked on generative foundation models at Apple. The startup has also recruited researchers and product designers from OpenAI, Stripe, and Netflix. Why does design matter so much to a company focused on AI training? Karanam says the startup has developed an interface that makes post-training more accessible to its nontechnical customers. articles.title: Apple’s inventory surges 154% as memory chip costs climb
articles.description: Apple says unprecedented memory chip costs will continue to rise, raising questions about future device prices as its inventory climbs to $14.5 billion.
articles.content: Apple’s stockpiling of inventory, particularly computer memory, continued in its fiscal fourth quarter, according to earnings reported Monday. The company reported that its inventory increased significantly in the quarter, growing from $11.09 billion in Q3 to $14.54 billion in Q4, a jump of 31.1%. Year-over-year, inventory grew 154.3% from $5.72 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025. Apple’s forecast of a 45% to 46% gross margin in the December quarter was largely attributed to the impact of higher memory costs. The company reported a gross margin of 47.9% for the September quarter. “What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” said Apple CEO John Ternus, speaking to analysts on the call. “As we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components.” He said that the company expected “even higher memory costs” in the December quarter, which would be partially offset by price increases implemented earlier this year on some devices, including Mac and iPad at the end of June and iPhones in September. Ternus also said that beyond December, Apple expects memory costs “continuing to increase.” “As we said before, we do believe we’ll see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time,” he noted, adding that the company was increasing its purchases of this key component. “As we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by 33 billion dollars from June to the September quarter, which you’ll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow.” Apple also brought COO Sabih Khan, who oversees the company’s supply chain and manufacturing, onto the call to address questions about memory. He reiterated the increased purchase obligations but did not rule out future price increases on Apple devices. The company also blamed supply constraints for weak iPad sales in the quarter. The iPad was one of the only product segments that didn’t grow, even as iPhone and Mac sales beat estimates. iPad revenue was $6.2 billion, below analysts’ expectations of $6.7 billion. articles.title: Why large dogs age faster than small ones, and other October research highlights
articles.description: Plus invisible tattoos, medieval skeleton gets an ID, trapping a single antimatter particle, and more.
articles.content: It’s a regrettable reality that there is never enough time to cover all the interesting scientific stories we come across. So every month, we highlight a handful of the best stories that nearly slipped through the cracks. October’s list includes an epigenetic mechanism for why large dogs age faster than smaller ones; physicists who trapped a single particle of antimatter for months; and invisible tattoo inks that only show up under UV light. Why large dogs age faster In many mammalian species, larger creatures tend to have longer lifespans. Mice, for instance, live an average of just two years, while some whales can last for as long as 200 years. Dogs, however, buck this pattern; larger dogs tend to age faster and die younger than smaller ones, which makes canines an ideal model for biologists to study to learn more about aging in general. Arizona State University scientists report that these lifespan differences seem to be due to so-called "jumping genes," according to a paper published in the journal Science. The authors used data from 864 dogs collected in the Dog Aging Project to map patterns of DNA methylation (which influences how much certain genes are turned on or off) across the entire genome. It's part of the epigenome, whose markers can change over time in response to stress and other environmental factors. Genetic sequences, by contrast, are largely fixed. So DNA methylation is a good chemical indicator of aging and DNA regulation.Read full article Comments

Lindsay Clancy returns to court in a bid to dismiss charges she killed her three young children
articles.description: Lindsay Clancy returns to court in a bid to dismiss charges she killed her three young children AP News Prosecutors ask judge to reject Lindsay Clancy defense’s motion to dismiss charges NBC News Prosecutors indicate plan to retry Lindsay Clancy for deaths of her three children BBC Lindsay Clancy is back in court for hearing about future of her criminal case ABC7 Los Angeles What's next in the Lindsay Clancy murder c
articles.content: PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — Lindsay Clancy ‘s lawyer urged a judge Monday to either the dismiss the murder charges against her, or get on with the business of putting her back on trial. This was the second time the Massachusetts mother has been in court since her first trial with ended with a deadlocked jury unable to agree whether she was legally responsible for killing her three young children. Jurors were split 11-1 in favor of acquittal when the judge declared a mistrial. Clancy’s defense team moved to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds, based on an unusual argument that the judge should have removed the one juror who favored conviction, then allowed jury deliberations to continue. Judge William Sullivan did not immediately rule on Monday. Clancy’s lawyer, Kevin Reddington, implored him to decide quickly, and also pressed the Plymouth District Attorney to reveal soon whether he plans to try Clancy on murder charges again. “I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year, or two or three,” Reddington said. Putting aside his sharp disagreement with the judge about the way the first trial ended, he said he wants Sullivan to preside over a second trial, if one happens. “I want a trial and I want it with you and I want it this spring.” Sullivan scheduled another hearing for Nov. 16 and suggested a retrial could begin in March. Prosecutors said they intend to retry Clancy if the case proceeds, but haven’t yet settled on whether they would pursue the same charges, or opt for a reduced charge that might be more palatable for the jury. Clancy’s lawyer has argued that she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behavior when she killed her three children in 2023. Prosecutors have acknowledged that Clancy had mental health problems, but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong. Reddington has staked part of his post-trial defense on assailing the one juror who wanted to convict Clancy. He urged the judge again on Monday to investigate that juror, whom he accused of being untruthful on his jury questionnaire and improperly using his cell phone during jury deliberations. At one point, Sullivan admonished Reddington to stop using the juror’s name in open court. Sullivan has a standing order sealing the names of the jurors temporarily to protect them from harassment — though several have done media interviews, including the holdout, Michael Desronvil. Reddington protested that the juror’s name “was all over the internet.” “Why don’t we all dial this back a little bit,” Sullivan said at one point. Another of Clancy’s lawyers, Martin Weinberg, argued Monday that a mistrial could have been avoided had the judge more thoroughly interrogated jurors about their breakdown in deliberations after the foreperson sent two notes indicating that the lone holdout wasn’t following the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt. After receiving the notes, Sullivan spoke with each juror, reminded them of their duties and explained what constitutes reasonable doubt. He asked whether they could apply the law to the case, and all said yes. Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague argued Monday that Sullivan had struck the right balance — and that pressing further would have required delving into the substance of the jury’s deliberations, which isn’t allowed. Desronvil said in a recent interview that he was certain of Clancy’s guilt, but other jurors wouldn’t listen. His lawyer, Heather O’Connor, urged the judge Monday not to investigate his conduct any further, saying he had simply done his duty as a juror. She disputed the allegations of improper cellphone use, saying all jurors were allowed to keep their phones and there was no evidence Desronvil had used his device to improperly research the case. “If that’s enough to put a juror under oath, to search their phone, to pull their history, then the lesson (for) every future juror in this Commonwealth is simple: Agree with the majority or potentially be investigated,” O’Connor said. Sullivan also heard arguments on the prosecutors’ request for a gag order while the case remains pending, to avoid influencing a future jury. Reddington gave interviews during the trial, while prosecutors generally did not speak to reporters. Clancy’s lawyers argued that it would amount to an unconstitutional restraint on speech. AP journalist Leah Willingham contributed from Boston.

articles.title: As a potential Democratic wave looms, Trump’s DOJ angles for last-minute power over midterms
articles.description: American democracy faces one of its biggest stress tests of the modern era, as President Donald Trump’s sprawling campaign for power over elections encounters a firewall of judges, state election workers and voting rights leaders heading into Election Day. A cascade of courtroom losses over the weekend dealt a major blow to the Trump administration’s […]
articles.content: President Donald Trump rallied with Iowa Republicans at the Five Flags Center in Dubuque on Nov. 1, 2026, two days before Election Day. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)American democracy faces one of its biggest stress tests of the modern era, as President Donald Trump’s sprawling campaign for power over elections encounters a firewall of judges, state election workers and voting rights leaders heading into Election Day. A cascade of courtroom losses over the weekend dealt a major blow to the Trump administration’s last-minute efforts ahead of Tuesday to assert authority over voting and hold the prospect of prosecutions over the heads of state election officials. But another round of last-minute court hearings was set for Monday — and the U.S. Department of Justice asked the U.S. Supreme Court to require California to set aside the ballots of 20,000 suspected noncitizens. Democrats, voting rights groups and even some former Trump administration officials have said they are braced for a range of possible disruptions and interference, especially as the president stares down the prospect of a blue wave that could wash away Republican control of Congress. Elections forecasters have said Democrats are on track to win control of the U.S. House and possibly the Senate, amid voter unhappiness with rising consumer costs. “I fully expect my former boss, Donald Trump, to try to steal this election,” Miles Taylor, a deputy Department of Homeland Security chief of staff during the first Trump administration who became an outspoken Trump critic, told reporters last week. Trump and his supporters have said the federal government’s actions are necessary to protect against noncitizen voting, which they warn cancels out the votes of Americans. While researchers have consistently found that noncitizen voting is rare and doesn’t impact the outcome of elections, Homeland Security has arrested dozens of noncitizens on allegations of election crimes in recent weeks, part of a concerted effort by the Trump administration to ramp up enforcement ahead of the election. The last-minute push, Trump allies note, comes after the Senate didn’t advance Trump’s signature election legislation, the SAVE America Act, which would have imposed stringent requirements on voters to show proof of citizenship. The legislation passed the House but faced bipartisan opposition in the Senate. “They voted against proof of citizenship so they can cheat,” Trump said during a rally in Salina, Kansas, on Sunday. In the past four days, a federal judge ordered the list of 20,000 suspected noncitizens in California shared with an immigrant rights group, which said Saturday it found major problems with its veracity. Another judge blocked the Justice Department from threatening election workers with prosecution. In Alaska, a judge dismissed a lawsuit that preemptively sought to question the certification of the results of Alaska’s U.S. Senate race. An appeals court also upheld limits on preelection field operations by Homeland Security. On Monday, judges were expected to weigh requests to restrict federal law enforcement agents from serving as election monitors and additional limits on armed federal personnel at polling locations. Federal law broadly prohibits armed federal troops or agents at election sites. Planning for ‘every single scenario’ As the court losses pile up, Democrats, civic leaders and election experts have watched with a wary eye toward how Trump will respond. Election preparations by critics of the Trump administration have been underway for months. Congressional Democrats have mapped out dozens of scenarios, including the possibility that Trump will falsely point to a foreign threat against U.S. elections as an excuse to disrupt voting or seize voting machines. They have also assembled a field army of volunteers to assist voters and monitor polling locations for signs of federal interference. Teams of lawyers have drafted a range of possible lawsuits that can be quickly filed if problems arise. Virginia Kase Solomón, president and CEO of the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, said her organization is deploying more than 21,000 election protection volunteers sporting bright yellow shirts. Common Cause has also trained 3,000 volunteers to work a voter hotline. “Common Cause is prepared for every single scenario and we are refusing to let fear win,” Kase Solomón said during a recent press briefing. Noncitizen voters The Trump administration’s actions follow a refusal by dozens of states, including California, to share their full voter roll that includes sensitive personal data — information the Trump administration says would allow it to identify noncitizen voters. “California could, but refuses to, provide the unredacted list, which would resolve this entire dispute in a matter of hours,” Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote on social media over the weekend. But Trump has spent years promoting falsehoods about stolen elections, long before the more recent focus on noncitizen voting. After he lost the 2020 election, the president and his allies waged an extensive pressure campaign in a bid to overturn his losses in key battleground states. Some supporters advanced baseless conspiracy theories about voting machines. As the midterm elections approach, Trump has again begun casting a cloud of suspicion over voting machines. He spoke about alleged vulnerabilities in the machines during a primetime speech in July, though in every state except Louisiana, machines produce paper records that can later be checked. In the final hours of the election, the president is returning to the theme. “You know the paper ballots cost 9% of what these crooked machines cost,” Trump said at a rally in Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday. Trump’s intensifying rhetoric has been matched by the Justice Department’s rapid-fire legal challenges over the past several days seeking to influence elections, which under the U.S. Constitution are run by the states. With polls set to open in a matter of hours, federal judges have blocked the Trump administration at every turn. Threats to election workers Late Friday, Judge Trina Thompson, an appointee of President Joe Biden in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, issued a temporary restraining order preventing the Trump administration from threatening election workers nationwide with prosecution. The order came after Essayli, during a court hearing last week, raised the possibility that California election officials could face “criminal liability” if they count the ballots of noncitizens. The Justice Department on Thursday also sent a letter to election officials nationwide that reiterated requirements under federal law to preserve election-related records and listed the criminal consequences of noncompliance. When election officials perform the work in the manner required by state and federal law, “they do not violate federal criminal law even if a particular ballot belongs” to an ineligible voter, Thompson wrote. The Justice Department has appealed the order to the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals. “Reminding election officials to follow federal law is a civic service, not a ‘threat,’” Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said on X. Supreme Court weighs ballots case Weeks after the Justice Department sued California in an effort to force election officials to set aside and not count the ballots of 20,000 voters it said were suspected noncitizens, the case reached the Supreme Court on Monday. “If it turns out that those individuals cast ballots but are not, in fact, U.S. citizens, then California’s counting of their votes will violate (federal law) and will debase or dilute valid votes cast by U.S. citizens,” U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in an emergency application to the high court. The Justice Department has so far failed in its effort to require California to set aside ballots from individuals on the list, which was compiled by Homeland Security based on checks of government records and use of the research service LexisNexis. A district court judge and the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals have both ruled against the Trump administration. An immigrant rights group raised serious concerns about the list over the weekend after a judge forced the Trump administration to share a copy with the organization. The Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA, said in a court filing Saturday that an analysis by data experts found that 42% of the names weren’t found on California’s current voter file. At least 22 names on the list are on a list of U.S. citizens compiled by the organization, the analysis found. Judge James Boasberg, an appointee of President Barack Obama in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, on Monday prohibited the Justice Department from demanding that California set aside ballots — echoing previous rulings in the case now before the Supreme Court. In Washington state, the Justice Department has demanded election officials set aside about 400 ballots from voters it alleges are noncitizens. On Sunday, several civil rights groups sued to block any segregation of ballots. “We are days away from Election Day and these threats, again, are an attempt to sow fear and throw out eligible votes with no transparency,” Lilliane Ballesteros, executive director of the Latino Community Fund of Washington state, said in a statement. Federal monitors at the polls On Sunday, the NAACP asked for a temporary restraining order to prevent a wide swath of federal law enforcement agents from serving as election monitors. The Justice Department has deployed election monitors for decades to watch polling places for compliance with federal voting rights laws. But the Trump administration has expanded the program, and plans to have roughly 1,000 monitors stationed across all 50 states on Election Day. Justice Department lawyers typically serve as monitors, but the Trump administration this year also plans to tap federal law enforcement agents. In a court filing, the NAACP alleged the deployments are illegal and will have a chilling effect that intimidates voters. “The law is clear — law enforcement agents can have an intimidating effect on voters, especially Black voters, and they have no role and no right to be inside our polling places,” Kristen Clarke, NAACP general counsel, said in a statement. The Justice Department said in a court document that monitors aren’t allowed to have firearms and have been instructed not to interfere with voting and must dress in business casual clothing. Senior Judge Reggie Walton, an appointee of President George W. Bush in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, held a hearing on Monday. The public docket indicated Walton would issue an order. Alaska challenge tossed Judge Sharon Gleason, an appointee of President Barack Obama in U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska, on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit that preemptively sought to pause certification of the Senate race. The DOJ wanted a certification pause if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan lost to Democrat Mary Peltola — and if Sullivan lost by less than the number of votes received by another candidate of the same name, Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported last week that Democrats worked to recruit Dan J. Sullivan, leading Trump to call for him and Peltola to be kicked out of the election. While Alaska election officials had initially tried to prevent Dan J. Sullivan from appearing on the ballot, the Alaska Supreme Court cleared his candidacy earlier this year. The Justice Department’s lawsuit had also asked for an order requiring all ballots for Dan J. Sullivan be set aside for further investigation. articles.content: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh. In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year. The increase in revenue follows the launch of Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup in September, which included a pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max model. The company raised prices across its older models at the same time. Apple also took the wraps off its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, but its preorder sales aren’t included in this earnings report. Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products. Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027. “We saw higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, and that was partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on non-memory components,” Apple CEO John Ternus said during an interview with CNBC. Apple reported a 12 percent increase in revenue overall, ballooning to $114.5 billion. Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales. Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks. It made a big push into the smart home space with its first smart home display and a series of video doorbells, security cameras, and door locks, made in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.
