articles.content: A person in Washington state has died from bird flu after exposure at an infected dairy farm, state health officials reported Sunday. It marks the third human bird flu death in the US since a strain of highly pathogenic (H5) avian influenza (HPAI) made the unprecedented jump from wild, migratory birds to dairy cows, which was first reported in the US in March 2024. The person who died was a Yakima County resident and was said to have had underlying health conditions, which could have made the person more vulnerable to the infection. On Friday, county officials reported that the person was severely ill and hospitalized. In the subsequent announcement of the person's death, officials said they would not be releasing further information about the person, including their name, gender, or age, out of respect for the family's privacy. "Our hearts go out to the individual's family and loved ones during this difficult time," Dave Atteberry, health officer for the Yakima Health District, said in a statement. "Avian influenza can cause severe illness, particularly among people who have underlying health conditions. While this is a serious and heartbreaking outcome, the risk to the general public remains low."Read full article Comments

articles.title: Mamdani’s progressive allies vie for seats in Congress
articles.content: Three New York City progressive Democrats are expected to win their midterm congressional races in Tuesday’s election. In June, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani stood before a packed house of voters, rallying support for a new wave of candidates hoping to build on his progressive momentum by winning seats in Congress. Inside Brooklyn’s historic Kings Theatre, the crowd answered chants of “Abolish ICE”, “Tax the rich” and “Free Palestine” with roaring applause, leaving little if any room for doubt about what the audience wanted from its politicians. Within days, all three congressional hopefuls endorsed by Mamdani – Claire Valdez, Brad Lander and Darializa Avila Chevalier – had won their Democratic primaries, becoming the party’s candidates in the midterm election. Lander, the former New York City comptroller, defeated Congressman Dan Goldman in a race in which Israel was the defining issue. Avila Chevalier, a community organiser, unseated longtime Congressman Adriano Espaillat. Valdez, a lawmaker in the New York State Assembly and member of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), won the contest to succeed retiring Congresswoman Nydia Velazquez. Both Valdez and Avila Chevalier had the backing of New York City’s DSA chapter. The candidates’ heavily Democratic districts mean they are likely to win congressional seats in Tuesday’s midterm elections. The June Democratic Party primaries effectively served as the main event for voters. In the final hours before Tuesday’s midterm election, New York City – a place colloquially dubbed the city that never sleeps – is more politically sleepy, with canvassers a bit harder to find than they were in the final stretch before the primaries. For the three progressive candidates, the past few months have been a test of how to turn bold campaign promises into policy they can actually deliver. The often slow minutiae of daily governance stand in stark contrast to buzzword-laden campaign slogans on the posters and signs galvanising their base of voters. The three congressional candidates’ platforms overlap on issues like abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), ending US military aid to Israel and establishing a public healthcare system dubbed Medicare for All. But their paths into progressive politics differ. Lander spent years in the New York City government, most recently as comptroller overseeing the city’s finances. After losing to Mamdani in the 2025 Democratic mayoral primary, he backed Mamdani in the election. But Lander’s congressional campaign against incumbent Goldman brought him national attention, with Israel and Palestine emerging as the defining issue in the race to lead a district with one of the largest Jewish populations in the United States. Lander has described Israel’s military campaign in Gaza as genocide and its occupation of Palestinian territory as apartheid. He also identifies as a Zionist who embraces pro-Palestinian activism, arguing that the positions are not mutually exclusive. Lander has long supported a two-state solution. “It’s straightforward that some approach to more shared safety for Israelis and Palestinians and for Jews and Muslims and everybody else here makes more sense,” Lander said. “I also want to be able to listen across those divides and have thoughtful policy debates.” Two weeks before Tuesday’s election, Israeli forces detained Lander in the occupied West Bank while he was volunteering to help with the olive harvest. Israeli authorities have since revoked his travel documents for a planned return visit. “The main story I come home with is not the story of my detention or the revocation of my travel authorisation,” Lander said. “The main story that I come with is the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the West Bank, which I just saw with my own eyes.” Lander has also long called for ICE to be abolished, including during President Donald Trump’s first term in office. Avila Chevalier’s political rise was similarly shaped by immigration and Palestinian rights, though she has taken a more uncompromising approach. After interning at a youth organisation in Nablus in the occupied West Bank in 2014, she returned to the US and became an advocate for Palestinian communities. Her “Babies Not Bombs” platform calls for redirecting military spending, including aid to Israel, towards domestic priorities such as childcare and healthcare. “It’s important for us to see our budgets as moral documents,” Avila Chevalier told Al Jazeera. “Our resources should be going towards the things that make our lives dignified and make our communities thrive – not towards war, not towards ICE or things that are harming our communities.” Valdez, meanwhile, came to progressive politics through the labour movement. A former union-organiser-turned-state-assemblymember, she supports stronger labour protections, including federal legislation such as the Protecting the Right to Organize (PRO) Act to make union organising easier. Valdez also backs national rent control and a government-run healthcare system to provide wider healthcare access than the country’s private-sector insurance model. “Public programmes and entitlements have been under attack by the right,” Valdez told Al Jazeera as she exited a polling location in her district on the first day of early voting. “I think not just clawing those back but really advancing a vision for what those things should be will be top priorities.” Abolishing ICE and ending military aid to Israel are lofty, ambitious goals, and neither is likely to be achieved without navigating competing interests in Congress and the White House. With the balance of congressional power potentially shifting towards Democrats in the midterms, the newcomers will have to decide which priorities to pursue first. That means looking for more immediate wins comparable to Mamdani’s move to fill 200,000 potholes when he took office as mayor, according to progressive political strategist Nomiki Konst. “[Get] on the same page about an issue that we all agree on and leverage that in the Democratic Congress because there’s no better time than the beginning,” Konst told Al Jazeera. For Lander, one such measure is banning members of Congress from trading individual stocks. “Maybe that restores a little bit of trust,” Lander said. “People say that’s gross that members of Congress trade stocks. At least this new Congress is doing something, you know, to show me they’re not just all in it for themselves.” Lander also sees an opportunity to restore enhanced government subsidies that expired at the end of 2025, raising premiums for many people who buy their private-sector insurance plans individually. “We can say we’re not going to pass a budget that doesn’t do that and force Republicans to vote one way or the other and see what Trump does,” Lander said. For Avila Chevalier, an early priority would be her “Babies Not Bombs” agenda, redirecting funding towards domestic needs. Valdez wants to pass the PRO Act. The three would not be the first progressive New Yorkers to enter Congress promising major change. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez won her legislative seat in 2018 by defeating longtime incumbent Joe Crowley. Since then, she has occasionally worked with Republicans on shared priorities. In 2025, Ocasio-Cortez introduced legislation with Republican Representative Anna Paulina Luna of Florida to cap credit card interest rates at 10 percent, echoing a proposal from Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri. The question, Konst says, is whether Mamdani’s endorsed candidates can turn ideological commitments into legislative results. Doing so will require compromise, including setting aside some priorities to advance others. Avila Chevalier is under the microscope after calling for New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch to resign over a man being shot in his car by ICE while his child was in the backseat. Avila Chevalier said she was later shoved to the ground by New York City police officers during protests following the shooting. Mamdani reportedly appointed Tisch on the recommendation of Governor Kathy Hochul, whose support was important to Mamdani’s mayoral campaign. An Atlantic magazine report suggested that her endorsement of Mamdani, whose more progressive platform included universal childcare and government-operated grocery stores, hinged on Tisch’s appointment. “Everybody wants to have their agenda passed, right? I think being really thoughtful about when to hold fire, when to fire, when to be bold, when to hold back, and when to say what you feel so you’ll get the most support,” Konst said. But Avila Chevalier said she is willing to work with anyone to advance her priorities. “There is always something that two people can agree on. And that’s where I plan on starting because I think organising is about meeting people where they’re at,” Avila Chevalier said. “There are so many folks who really want to see healthcare transformed in this country, who really want to see a moratorium on data [centres]. That is a bipartisan issue for so many.”

articles.title: After sex, many girls and young women try to avoid pregnancy with unproven methods
articles.description: To prevent pregnancy after sex, U.S. teenage girls and young women are more likely to rely on unproven strategies such as prayer, exercise and jumping up and down than they are on evidence-based methods such as Plan B emergency contraception, according to a new study. The study, published in The Journal of Sex Research, is […]
articles.content: A teacher holds a student’s baby while his class completes coursework at a high school for young parents in Spokane, Wash. A new study finds that many girls and young women try to avoid pregnancy after sex with unproven methods. (Photo by Camilla Forte/The Hechinger Report)To prevent pregnancy after sex, U.S. teenage girls and young women are more likely to rely on unproven strategies such as prayer, exercise and jumping up and down than they are on evidence-based methods such as Plan B emergency contraception, according to a new study. The study, published in The Journal of Sex Research, is based on a survey of 1,259 girls and women between the ages of 15-29. A quarter of the 633 respondents who reported having sexual intercourse and were not pregnant said they had used a post-coital method to prevent pregnancy. Of those, about 9% said they’d used evidence-based emergency birth control such as Plan B or a copper intrauterine device. But about 16% used methods without proven efficacy, including prayer (9.4%), douching (6%), jumping up and down or exercising (3.3%), ingesting something by mouth (1.9%), punching one’s stomach or uterus (1.4%), taking medicine or vitamins (0.9%), inserting something vaginally (0.5%), or using an enema (0.2%). About one-fifth of this group used more than one method — praying and douching being the most common combination. These types of methods were more common among minors and non-white respondents. “There is a need to better understand what is underlying these practices or the use of these strategies,” said Riley J. Steiner, an associate professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and one of the authors of the study. “We really don’t want young people to be seen as misguided or to be judged for these practices,” she said. “They’re trying things, and so how do we best support them to meet what their goals are?” The release of the study comes on the heels of the Trump administration cutting and reshaping programs such as Title X and the Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program, created to lower the rate of unintended pregnancy and to inform people of safe and effective options for preventing pregnancy. In August, a federal judge blocked the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services from implementing sweeping changes to grants under the Teen Pregnancy Prevention Program, amid an ongoing lawsuit brought by Hennepin County, Minnesota; King County, Washington; an Iowa Planned Parenthood affiliate; and SIECUS: Sex Ed for Social Change, a nonprofit advocacy group. However, grant funding that has already been cut won’t be restored for now, the judge ruled. The Trump administration has cast doubt on the safety of hormonal contraception, which is increasingly perceived as controversial on social media. “In our current environment where there’s a lot of mis- and disinformation online and structural constraints that make it hard to access medically evidenced contraceptive methods, it does make sense that people are behaving in broader ways to try to manage that risk,” Steiner said. But she also noted that the study found the lack of information on contraceptive methods was more likely to drive people to choose post-coital methods rather than concerns about hormones or an inability to obtain clinical care. Meanwhile, sex education varies widely across the country. And this year several states modified their sex education policies, according to an analysis by SIECUS. In Alabama, Republican Gov. Kay Ivey signed a law requiring sex education to be focused on promoting “sexual risk avoidance,” updated terminology for “abstinence-only” instruction. The law prohibits sex education before fourth grade and prohibits school districts from partnering with organizations that do not promote “sexual risk avoidance,” as well as organizations that provide or promote abortion. Instructors are prohibited from teaching students about birth control, but parents can opt out of sex education classes. Currently, 15 states offer abstinence-only sex education, according to SIECUS. In Wisconsin, Democratic Gov. Tony Evers signed a law requiring instruction on adoption as part of sex education. In Arizona, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs vetoed a bill that would have required instruction on adoption and newborn safe-haven laws whenever contraception or sexually transmitted infections are mentioned. The state already requires instruction to refer to adoption and parenting as the “preferred choice” over abortion. Three states – Alabama, Louisiana and South Dakota – enacted laws requiring or requesting instruction on fetal development in schools or the viewing of a fetal ultrasound or animated video, such as the “Baby Olivia” video developed by anti-abortion groups. In California, Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom signed bills requiring instruction on human trafficking and dating abuse and digital violence. articles.title: Two fishermen rescued after boat capsizes in Lake St. Clair
articles.content: Two fishermen were treated for a slight case of hypothermia Monday afternoon after they were pulled out of Lake St. Clair near Gino’s Surf, according to firefighters. According to the Macomb County Sheriff’s Office, deputies received a repot of a capsized vessel about 2:20 p.m. The sheriff’s marine division responded to the scene and rescued the two individuals, deputies said. Battalion Chief Chris Durso of the Harrison Township Fire Department said the fishermen, both township residents, were angling from a 10- to 14-foot aluminum boat when one man went to retrieve something. “As he went to grab something, the boat shifted and began to take on water before it capsized,” Durso said. The sheriff’s marine division responded with their boat and were able to rescue the men from the water, he said. Durso said the two men were treated by an EMS team for a slight case of hypothermia and released. The water temperature of the lake was about 56 degrees, according to seatemperature.info.

From Trump Country to Detroit: What to watch as Michigan votes
articles.description: These are the regions, trends and races to watch as Michigan election results come in on Tuesday night.
articles.content: Michigan voters to decide key races for the U.S. Senate, governor, Congress and state Legislature Turnout could be revealing in southeast Michigan, rural Trump Country, college towns and West Michigan Two statewide ballot proposals could also offer clues about voters’ frustration with government and political influence Michigan campaign stops, television ads, text messages and robocalls are poised to end Tuesday as election results begin rolling in. Get ready for information overload. Shortly after polls close at 8 p.m., Michigan’s vast network of local clerks will begin posting partial results online. Breathless prognostication will ensue as pundits fill air time with explanations about what it all means. What’s worth your time and attention? Here are some of the regions, trends and races that Bridge Michigan reporters will be closely watching on Tuesday night. The battle for southeast Michigan Democrats have made significant gains in Oakland County as moderates cooled on President Donald Trump, but moods here could again be pivotal – especially in the US Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers. Democratic U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who represents the region in the U.S. House, endorsed Rogers on Sunday. Related: Michigan election rules, races and results: 10 things to know about Nov. 3 Election integrity takes center stage in Michigan governor’s race Fact checks: What’s true, false in Michigan governor’s race Keep an eye on what happens in Rochester and Rochester Hills, where Republicans have maintained a narrow edge in recent years despite Democrats’ best efforts, along with communities with large Jewish populations like Bloomfield Hills, West Bloomfield, Southfield, Oak Park and Huntington Woods. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., left, her fiance Jason Turkish, right, stand with Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, second left, and his wife Kristi Rogers during a church service at Perfecting Church, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Jose Juarez) In Wayne County, whether Black voters in Detroit who supported Stevens turn out to vote for El-Sayed could prove pivotal for his chances. And in nearby Dearborn and other communities with large Arab American populations, some voters who supported Trump in 2024 over concerns about the Biden administration’s actions in the Middle East are souring on the GOP amid inflammatory rhetoric from the GOP around El-Sayed’s Muslim heritage. Stevens won both counties in the primary, and many of the region’s Jewish voters have made their concerns with El-Sayed known. But if Democrats successfully turn Stevens’ defection into a rallying cry that boosts turnout among party faithful, the move could ultimately backfire. — Lauren GibbonsDonate Trump Country Are there truly MAGA-Abdul voters? A major gambit in El-Sayed’s campaign is the belief that his populist economic message can bring over enough of the MAGA base to forge a new(-ish) electoral coalition, offsetting whatever inroads Rogers might’ve made with moderates turned off by El-Sayed’s progressivism. Some Democrats believe it’s their best chance to earn back the support of some of the rural, working-class voters they ceded to the GOP over the past 20 to 30 years. US Sen. Bernie Sanders campaigning in Alpena and El-Sayed’s Escanaba rally are just a couple examples of their efforts. At the same time, Republicans and the outside groups supporting them on the ground have again targeted low-propensity voters, hoping to recreate the 2024 magic that helped Trump carry Michigan by 80,000 votes. “Pretend I’m on the ballot” is the president’s closing message to supporters in Michigan, but there’s big demographic overlap in who the Senate campaigns are targeting, and how rural Michigan votes this week could have big implications for Michigan politics. There are swathes of ruby-red Trump Country all over Michigan worth watching. Look north, like in Otsego County (67% Trump in ‘24) and in the Upper Peninsula’s Delta County (65% Trump), where El-Sayed rallied. For a more suburban perspective, watch Livingston County (61% Trump) not just for the Senate results, but whether progressive Will Lawrence’s anti-data center message can make a dent against US Rep. Tom Barrett in the 7th Congressional District. And keep an eye on Ottawa County, which Trump carried by more than 20 percentage points in 2024. Like much in politics, it’s a game of inches. The likelihood El-Sayed carries any of these counties is slim-to-none; it’s the shifts, if any, that are worth watching. You could compare the results to past elections, but it’s El-Sayed’s performance relative to Jocelyn Benson, his Democrat counterpart at the top of the ticket, that should be most informative. If El-Sayed significantly outperforms Benson, who is by most accounts a more palatable candidate to the modern Democratic coalition, in any part of Michigan’s Trump Country, Democrats with their eye on 2028 are certain to take notice. — Simon Schuster What do the youth do? El-Sayed is banking on youth enthusiasm to boost his campaign. He’s spent considerable time on college campuses and has worked to stay relevant to younger voters through new media appearances and prolific social media use. Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters during a campaign rally at Eastern Michigan University, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, in Ypsilanti, Mich. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) Michigan is home to about 937,000 residents ages 18-24, many of whom are concentrated in East Lansing, Ann Arbor and other college towns. Not all are registered to vote, and turnout among those who are has historically been fickle. But the state’s young voters have at times made a big difference for candidates — think Barack Obama in 2008 and Sanders’ surprise primary win in 2016. Rogers has consistently polled better among older voters, a group that can be reliably counted on to cast ballots. If El-Sayed wants to counteract that advantage, he’ll need to run up the numbers in counties like Ingham and Washtenaw, which helped put him over the edge in the primary. — Lauren Gibbons Battle for Lansing The governor’s race between Benson and Republican John James will decide who replaces term-limited Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. But how much either of them win by — or how long their proverbial coattails are — could also help decide control of the state Legislature, where Republicans currently control the House and Democrats control the state Senate, each by slim margins. All 148 seats are on the ballot. In the battle for the Michigan Senate, both major parties are fighting for the 13th Senate District seat in Oakland County that is held by Democratic Sen. Rosemary Bayer, who chose not to seek reelection. Her Senate district was redrawn following litigation, and this is the first election cycle the map (which is as close to a 50/50 split as you can get) will be tested. A win for Republicans here could indicate just how competitive new Senate maps can be. As for the state House, I’ll be watching a couple races in metro Detroit, where Democrats are hoping to flip an open seat in the 54th District (Oakland County) but Republicans are hoping to flip an open seat in the 31st (Wayne County). Both parties consider those must-wins. I’ll also be watching the 86th Michigan House District race in west Michigan, where incumbent GOP Rep. Nancy DeBoer of Holland is facing a challenge from Republican-turned-Democrat Joseph McClusky. If Republicans don’t turn out the vote in areas they’ve won by double digits in the past, it could be a sign of GOP struggles elsewhere. — Jordyn Hermani Key congressionals The road to flipping the US House runs through Michigan, and Democrats are optimistic they’ll flip GOP seats in the 4th, 7th and 10th congressional districts. In the 4th and 7th districts, I’ll be watching college turnout at Western and Michigan State University, respectively, as political onlookers have told me big returns from these areas could mean a good night for Democrats. In the Macomb County-based 10th District, turnout in the cities of Center Line and Eastpointe will be especially important because it could illustrate whether Republican efforts to grow manufacturing – which the area is heavily associated with – are enough to overcome Democrats’ messaging that Trump’s tariffs have increased voters’ everyday cost of living. — Jordyn Hermani Shifting regions In his 2024 bid for the Senate, Rogers and now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin nearly tied in Saginaw and Slotkin won Genesee County by 8 points. Once considered a Democratic stronghold, this region has become significantly more competitive in recent election cycles. Muskegon County, where Rogers spent time campaigning Friday, presents a similar opportunity for Republicans. If the GOP continues to make inroads in these three counties, that’s good news for Rogers. El-Sayed and other Democrats, meanwhile, stand to gain from demographic shifts elsewhere in West Michigan as Kent County, home to Grand Rapids, and northwest Michigan counties like Grand Traverse and Leelanau become more Democratic. — Lauren Gibbons The proposals! Are you a voter who doesn’t closely follow the news or isn’t terminally online, yet is broadly angry or dissatisfied about the current state of politics and government? There are two proposals on the statewide ballot that may appeal to you, and I’ll be watching them closely to gauge how Michigan voters are feeling. Even as affordability has dominated the dialogue this election, more than 85% of likely Michigan voters agree with the statement “wealthy people and corporations have too much influence over government,” according to a recent MSU poll. Supporters have centered that message as they promote Proposal 2, which would attempt to bar state government contractors, regulated utilities and their executives from donating to political candidates in Michigan. The measure is likely to pass — and on a broadly bipartisan basis — but is also expected to face legal challenges as opponents try to use courts to block implementation. Proposal 1, a question of whether Michigan should convene a convention of delegates to potentially rewrite the whole state constitution, may be more electorally interesting. It’s on the ballot every 16 years, has been rejected by voters before and is unlikely to pass. But anger at our political system writ large has shown no signs of abating, and Tuesday’s results could be an indication of how much steam a “tear-it-all-down” mentality has gained among the electorate. I’ll hedge this prognostication by noting that the result may just reflect how effective a few million dollars in anti-”con con” messaging has been. There is no organized push for a convention, but an alliance of special interests has united to oppose it through an ironically named committee, Protect MI Constitution from Special Interests. — Simon Schuster

articles.title: Michigan election rules, races and results: 10 things to know about Nov. 3
articles.description: What you need to know about voting rules, key races and when to expect results from Michigan’s Nov. 3 election.
articles.content: Michigan’s Nov. 3 midterm election will determine the state’s next governor, US senator and more Polls will open Tuesday from 7 am to 8 pm. Absentee ballots can still be returned in-person but it’s too late to mail them Read on to see what’s on your ballot, as well as what you need to bring to the polls on Tuesday LANSING — Election Day is Tuesday, and Michiganders will have the chance then to decide not just their next US Senator, but who will represent them in the state House, Senate and, in some cases, at the local level. The general election will also help determine majority control of Congress, as well as who succeeds term-limited Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat. Voters will also weigh in on a ballot proposal aiming to bar political spending in state elections by Michigan’s regulated utilities and large government contractors, and another on whether to hold the state’s first constitutional convention since the 1960s. Related: Governor race fact checks: What’s true, false about Jocelyn Benson, John James US Senate fact checks: What’s true, false about Abdul El-Sayed, Mike Rogers All Bridge Michigan fact checks of candidates, ballot proposals As of 7 a.m. Monday, more than 2.3 million Michiganders had already cast absentee ballots or voted early in person, about 31% of all active registered voters, according to the state. That includes 1.6 million absentee ballots and 743,450 ballots cast during Michigan’s early in-person voting period, which ended Sunday. Check out the Bridge Michigan voter guide for more information on candidates, top issues and more. Here’s what else you need to know: What’s on my ballot, and where can I vote? Michiganders will see different candidates and races on the ballot depending on where they live, but all voters will have the chance to vote on a number of statewide positions. To see what’s on your ballot, click here. Don’t know your precinct? Click here. Polls are open from 7 am to 8 pm on Election Day, though voters in line by 8 pm on Tuesday can still cast a ballot. It’s too late to participate in early in-person voting, which ended Sunday. If you have an absentee ballot, it’s also probably too late to mail it. Instead, return it to a drop box or your local clerk’s office by 8 p.m. Tuesday. What do I need to bring to vote? Bring a photo ID such as a driver’s license, state ID, US passport, military ID, student ID or tribal ID. If you don’t have one, you can still vote by signing an affidavit confirming your identity.Donate Not registered to vote? Eligible residents can still register and vote on Election Day at their local clerk’s office until 8 p.m. Bring proof of residency, such as a state ID, utility bill, paycheck or government document. To register, you must: Be a US citizen Be at least 18 years old Have lived in your city or township for at least 30 days Not be currently serving a jail or prison sentence Once your eligibility is verified, you can submit a registration application to the clerk. Are there accommodations for voters with disabilities? Michigan requires a number of accommodations for those with disabilities to vote. The state has a separate ombudsman office to ease accessibility during elections. You can also ask another person to assist you in completing your ballot, though this person cannot be your employer, an agent of your employer or a person associated with your workplace’s labor union, if applicable. For more information, click here. Key state-level races Top statewide offices and all legislative seats are on the ballot this year in Michigan, including: Governor: Democrat Jocelyn Benson and Republican John James are battling to succeed term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Benson is benefiting from backlash against the Trump administration. James, meanwhile, is counting on Michigan voters to oscillate back to the GOP by persuading voters that Whitmer, Benson and other Democrats are to blame for the state’s trajectory. Jocelyn Benson as Secretary of State: What does her record show? John James in the US House: What does his record show? Legislature: Control of the Michigan Legislature is on the line as both major political parties fight to win majorities. Democrats currently hold a 20-18 seat advantage in the state Senate, while Republicans have a 58-52 edge in the House. 10 races to watch in battle for Michigan Legislature There are also a number of other consequential races, including: Attorney General: Doug Lloyd (R) vs. Eli Savit (D) Secretary of State: Anthony Forlini (R) vs. Garlin Gilchrist II (D) Michigan Supreme Court: Meet the candidates State Board of Education: Meet the candidates Key federal races Michigan has a number of competitive federal races to watch this cycle, including: US Senate: The race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers is one of the nation’s most closely watched races — and most expensive — a tossup that could determine which party controls Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump’s term. Abdul El-Sayed under microscope: His record, from public health to podcasts Mike Rogers wants a job in the US Senate. What’d he do in the House? Congress: There are several competitive races for the US House in Michigan that could play a role in whether Republicans keep their majority. Among them: In Mid-Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, incumbent Republican US Rep. Tom Barrett is challenged by Democrat Will Lawrence, a progressive environmental activist and community organizer In Macomb County’s 10th Congressional District, Republican US Army Capt. Michael Bouchard and Democratic prosecutor Christina Hines are competing to fill the seat being vacated by James Southwest Michigan’s 4th US House District, where incumbent GOP US Rep. Bill Huizenga faces a challenge from Democratic state Sen. Sean McCann What about the statewide ballot questions? Depending on jurisdiction, Michiganders may have a handful of questions on their individual ballots, but these two will be on all ballots statewide: Proposal 1 of 2026: This asks voters whether they want to convene a constitutional convention, a question that automatically appears on the ballot every 16 years and has been defeated in prior elections. Proposal 2 of 2026: This would prohibit direct or indirect contributions to Michigan politicians by DTE Energy, Consumers Energy and companies with more than $250,000 in state government contracts, along with immediate family members and other people with close connections to the companies. When will we know race results? It’s difficult to predict. Bridge Michigan doesn’t call races, but instead relies on The Associated Press (AP) to declare winners. In some races, results may not be known until early Wednesday, Nov. 4. Keep checking in with Bridge on election night for the latest info. How long does vote counting usually take? In the 2024 general election, the AP first reported results at 8:06 p.m. ET, or six minutes after polls closed in most of the state. The vote count reached the halfway mark at 12:12 a.m. ET. The last vote update of the night was at 4:40 a.m. ET with about 99% of total votes counted. The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, Bridge will continue to cover newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. But we’ll make clear the AP has not yet declared a winner and explain why. When are early and absentee votes released? Michigan counties vary in how and when they release vote results. The first vote updates of the night across the state are expected to include a mix of results from absentee, early in-person and Election Day voting. Wayne, Oakland, Macomb, Kent, Genesee and Washtenaw counties tend to release relatively few results in their first vote updates. What triggers a recount? Recounts in Michigan are automatic in statewide races if the vote margin is 0.1% or less of the total votes cast. Under the state’s 2024 recount law, candidates may request and pay for a recount if they have a “good-faith belief” that there’s a “reasonable chance” they would have won if not for a vote-counting error.

articles.title: How late Detroit techno pioneer Juan Atkins redefined electronic music
articles.description: Juan Atkins, who died at 64, is widely credited with creating and popularizing the genre of music out of Detroit known around the world as techno.
articles.content: SÃO PAULO, SP - 20.05.2023: C6 FEST EM SÃO PAULO - North American DJ and producer Juan Atkins presents the Model 500 Live show during the C6 Fest in São Paulo on May 20, 2023, at Ibirapuera Park.((Photo: Yuri Murakami/Fotoarena/Sipa USA))Detroit techno godfather Juan Atkins died over the weekend. He was 64.Atkins is widely recognized in the music industry, and among fans of the genre, as the originator of Detroit’s techno music. Along with two collaborators - Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson - Atkins formed the roots of the genre in 1983. Together, they were known as the Belleville Three.Atkins released nine albums of music, first as a part of the duo Cybotron and then under the alias Model 500.Atkins’ vision for electronic futurism went on to become a global phenomenon.“It was music born out of technology basically, and produced from all electronic instruments and also computers and sequencers and drum computers and everything that developed out of the technological movement,” Atkins told Michigan Public in an interview in 2015.Atkins was inspired by futurism and a society that was transitioning from an industrial world to an age of technological growth. He said he believed music should reflect that transformation and even help prepare people for the future.Growing up in and around Detroit, he saw technology reshaping the auto industry. At the same time, he embraced synthesizers, drum machines, and electronic sounds to imagine what this new world might sound like.Techno music is now especially popular in many parts of Europe, and is celebrated each Memorial Day weekend at Movement Electronic Music Festival (formerly known as Detroit Electronic Music Festival).“When it comes to music, specifically electronic music, the atmosphere is unmatchable anywhere else. I mean, Detroit is like no other place in terms of creativity,” Atkins said in 2015.Tributes to Atkins poured out on social media among Detroit’s musicians and creators. Most notable among them were the two men who, with Atkins, composed the Belleville Three.“Juan was the originator of Techno, a true visionary who opened the door for so many of us, myself included,” Saunderson said in a statement on his personal Instagram page. “We shared a journey that changed music forever, and I’ll always be grateful for his friendship, guidance and everything he gave to our scene.“He never mentioned how sick he was for years. He just went out and did his job as best he could,” May said in a video statement on his personal Instagram page. “Respect his legacy, respect the effort, respect the work, respect the accomplishments.”

Michigan State Board of Education candidates weigh in on key issues ahead of election
articles.description: Two of eight seats are open this election cycle within the Michigan State Board of Education. WDET spoke to five candidates head of the Nov. 3 election. The post Michigan State Board of Education candidates weigh in on key issues ahead of election appeared first on WDET 101.9 FM.
articles.content: Two of eight seats are open this election cycle within the Michigan State Board of Education. WDET spoke to five candidates head of the Nov. 3 election. Four major-party candidates and one libertarian are running for two open seats at the Michigan’s State Board of Education. The two elected candidates will help lead education policy for Michigan’s 1.4 million public school students for the next eight years. WDET’s Abby Harris and Angela Martinez spoke to candidates Judith Pritchett (D, incumbent), Terrence Collins (R), Bree Moeggenberg (R), current board vice-president chair Tiffany Tilley (D, incumbent) and Charles Essner (L) to discuss their education stances and goals ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3, 2026. Judith Pritchett is running for re-election for one of the two at-large seats open on the Michigan State Board of Education. Pritchett says she wants to see academic progress in Michigan schools. “We don’t want to ignore the fact that we are not seeing the improvements that we would like to see in mathematics, social studies and science.” Pritchett also would like to improve access to career technical education and increase support for special needs students. Pritchett mentioned how important it is to have small class sizes in Michigan schools. “The smaller the class sizes, the better teachers are able to assist students who may be struggling or who are ahead of the curve.” Terrence Collins is running for one of the two at-large seats open on the Michigan State Board of Education. Collins says disciplinary policies need to change. “We’ve moved towards restorative practices and away from just standard disciplinary practices. We’re allowing too many distractions to go back to our classrooms day after day. Our teachers are struggling.” He also says he would like to improve student literacy and bring back civics education. Collins is one of two Republicans in the race. Collins believes technology policies in school need to change. “I’d really like to see no technology in our elementary schools but very limited technology in our middle schools and then the (full) introduction of those technologies in high schools.” Collins also said he would like to improve student literacy and bring back civics education to classrooms. The State Board of Education’s co-vice president is seeking reelection. Tiffany Tilley has served on the board since 2018. She says she has worked to improve graduation rates and to make literacy training mandatory for K-5 educators. Tilley says improving students’ literacy is still a priority for the board. “The work is being done on the state level, but we need to continue to do the work. However, chronic absenteeism is really hurting the literacy rate here in Michigan. We have to make sure that we are helping our parents, supporting our parents, and getting those babies in those seats.” Tilley also notes that she wants to continue her work improving special education supports and addressing the shortage of teachers if reelected. Tilley has a wide range of education experience as a substitute teacher, early childhood educator, a STEM instructor at Wayne State University and more. Tilley worked to make reading training mandatory for K-5 educators to help improve literacy skills for students across the state. That will take effect in 2031. The state board sets policies and standards for education but has no oversight of local districts’ day-to-day operations. Still, Tilley says feedback is important. “We welcome public comment. We want to hear what’s going on, the good and the bad. A lot of the work is done on a local level. However, we do want to support parents and students and educators that have concerns and any way that we can fill in the gap.” If reelected, Tilley says she wants to continue working on special education support, literacy improvements along with addressing ongoing teacher shortages. Moggenberg has been a licensed childcare provider for nearly two decades and worked at Great Start Readiness programs in Isabella County. Moggenberg said her top priority is to prevent people from leaving Michigan’s public schools. “We need to stop the bleed. We need to stop the drop of parents leaving, teachers leaving, and students being in the classroom and just simply being checked out, and I think the number one way to do that is we have to restore instructional focus. Our classrooms need to be neutral, they need to be reliable, and they need to be stable.” Moggenberg says the current board’s focus on literacy improvement is important. However, she also states that she rarely hears discussion about providing more help in classrooms to help younger students. “We have to start looking at the individual needs of students when they are very young, and when we build those up, then that science of reading is really going to start sinking in, and we’ll see our proficiency rates start to rise. If we want them to continue to grow, we have to give them the skills to be able to do that.” Other key priorities for Moggenberg include building partnerships with parents, figuring out ways to prevent schools closing from low enrollment and how to keep sexuality and gender politics out of classrooms. Libertarian Charles Essner is running for a seat on the state’s board of education. Essner has a background in engineering. He wants to be an advocate for families and local communities. Essner believes the state’s funding needs to be fixed. “The funding needs to be kept local. It needs to not come with strings. We need to change how funding is ultimately done, because right now it simply removes the power from local community and the parents from actually having the school that they think their children need.” Essner believes educators and local communities should be the ones making decisions for their schools, not the state. *Editor’s note: Above coverage aired from Oct. 23-26, 2026.

articles.title: Opinion | Michigan college students are registered to vote. What happens next?
articles.description: Registration is a milestone, and participation is the necessary outcome. College students may find the distance between the two can be surprisingly difficult to navigate, but we should not confuse those barriers with indifference. At Grand Valley, we have seen what is possible when we approach voter participation intentionally.
articles.content: With the midterm election upon us, universities in Michigan and across the country should be asking a question that goes beyond who will win on Tuesday: How many of our students who are registered to vote will actually cast a ballot, both in this election and in the years ahead? Philomena V. Mantella is president of Grand Valley State University. (Courtesy photo) At Grand Valley State University, the numbers reveal progress, challenges to overcome and the profound opportunity to establish a lifetime of civic participation. In the 2022 midterms, 87% of our eligible students were registered to vote. Yet only 53% of those registered actually voted. Nearly 9 in 10 had cleared the first hurdle. Almost half of those registered never crossed the finish line. The easy explanation is that young people are apathetic or disengaged from democracy. However, the data suggest a more complicated story. Students who take the initiative to register have demonstrated an intention to participate, yet something changes between that intention and casting a ballot. That gap deserves our attention. This is not a problem unique to Grand Valley. According to Tufts University’s National Study of Learning, Voting, and Engagement, 76% of eligible college students were registered for the 2022 midterms, yet only 30.6% of those students voted. That means roughly 6 in 10 registered college students did not cast a ballot. Even in the higher-profile 2024 presidential election, 76% of eligible college students were registered, but only 70% voted. Nearly 1 in 3 registered students still did not participate. These numbers point to an important distinction: Registration is a milestone, and participation is the necessary outcome. College students may find the distance between the two can be surprisingly difficult to navigate. Students may be managing temporary addresses, unfamiliar voting procedures, class schedules, employment obligations and uncertainty about where or how to vote. We should not confuse those barriers with indifference. We should also not assume that eliminating practical obstacles alone will solve every dimension of civic disengagement. Trust in institutions, confidence that participation matters and a sense of personal agency are also essential. At Grand Valley, we have seen what is possible when we approach voter participation intentionally. In the 2014 midterm election, just 14.8% of our eligible students voted. By 2022, participation had climbed to 46.2%, well above the national average of 30.6%. Perhaps more telling, between the 2018 and 2022 midterms, student voting nationally declined by approximately 8.5 percentage points. At Grand Valley, it increased by approximately 11 points. To achieve this, we did not simply ask students to register. We worked to make voting more accessible. We brought a satellite township clerk’s office into our student center, helping students navigate the practical requirements of participation. We encouraged students in classrooms to develop a plan to vote. On Election Day, we provided transportation to polling locations used by our students. Michigan’s expansion of voting access has also helped create opportunities for participation. Our progress cannot be attributed to campus practices alone. The data also demonstrates that we are far from finished. To go further, we must understand what is concealed by averages. Our 2022 data revealed participation differences of more than 20 percentage points across racial groups and nearly 30 points across academic fields. Those differences deserve examination. We need to understand where students encounter barriers, where engagement is strongest and what approaches are effective. We know how to approach complex student success challenges. Michigan’s universities build systems to understand attrition, support retention, degree completion and career readiness. We measure outcomes, identify barriers, design interventions and examine where progress is uneven. The opportunity to apply these same capabilities to advancing civic participation is right in front of us.Donate Addressing practical barriers, however, is only the first part of the work. Building a sense of agency in our democracy is the second, and arguably more important, endeavor. Universities can help students move from non-participation to registration and from registration to voting. However, the opportunity for lifetime impact is even greater. We can help students develop the mindset and durable capacities that make civic participation meaningful to them: evaluating information, considering competing perspectives, exercising independent judgment and understanding how individual actions contribute to societal outcomes. Also critically important, this work must be rigorously nonpartisan. Our responsibility is not to tell students what to think, which candidates to support or how to vote. It is to equip them with the knowledge, judgment, confidence and practical means to make those decisions for themselves. Nonpartisanship does not limit this work, it makes it legitimate. We can continue to treat civic participation as an optional activity, celebrating registrations while accepting the gap between intention and action, or we can recognize it as an essential dimension of an empowered education. Beyond Election Day, universities still have opportunities to help students translate intention into participation. More importantly, our responsibility should not end when the polls close. We should examine our registration-to-voting conversion rates, identify disparities among student populations and evaluate which institutional practices made a difference. Above all, we should commit to developing the skills, confidence and sense of agency that empower students to participate fully in our democracy — not just in one election, but throughout their lives.

(Wyatt Gordon/The Virginia Mercury)Fewer than 1 in 20 rental listings across the largest U.S. cities are flagged as reserved for renters under an income limit, according to new data from Apartments.com. But average income-restricted rent fell year over year in 13 of the 50 markets, compared with three for market-rate rent. Just 4.6% of listings across the 50 largest metro areas were listed as “income-restricted” in the third quarter of this year, whether through public housing, a housing voucher or as a tax-credit property, the report by the rental listing site said. The finding was based on a sample of more than 70,000 active listings out of the site’s full inventory of over a million apartments. Washington, D.C., while being one of the most expensive housing markets in the country, has the most available income-restricted units at 227, the report said. San Antonio, Texas, had the highest share of income-restricted listings, at 12.4% of its total listings, followed by Austin at 11.7% and then two Virginia cities: Richmond and Norfolk at 10%. On the other end of the spectrum, the San Francisco Bay area stood at 4.2%. Income-restricted rents average $988 per month in Detroit, the lowest price among the 50 markets measured. Averaged across all 50 metros, income-restricted rent came to $1,448 a month in the third quarter. Market-rate rent averaged $1,756. Proposed changes to federal housing assistance programs could further affect the income-restricted market. Stateline previously reported that the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development has proposed allowing public housing authorities and certain property owners to impose work requirements and time limits on some rental assistance recipients. articles.title: Pohutsky calls Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers a ‘betrayal’ of reproductive rights
articles.description: For state Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia), the decision by U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens to endorse Republican Mike Rogers for U.S. Senate was a “betrayal” and “unconscionable,” a feeling shared by many Democrats — especially in terms of Rogers’ stance on abortion policy. “You either support reproductive rights or you support Mike Rogers. You can’t do both,” […]
articles.content: Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia) speaks ahead of Gov. Gretchen Whitmer signing the last bill in the Reproductive Health Act in Lansing on Dec. 11, 2023. (Photo: Anna Liz Nichols)For state Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia), the decision by U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens to endorse Republican Mike Rogers for U.S. Senate was a “betrayal” and “unconscionable,” a feeling shared by many Democrats — especially in terms of Rogers’ stance on abortion policy. “You either support reproductive rights or you support Mike Rogers. You can’t do both,” she told Michigan Advance on Monday, a day after Stevens stunned her Democratic colleagues and appeared with Rogers at a Detroit church and endorsed his candidacy over that of Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. Pohutsky said she and Stevens represented overlapping areas before Michigan’s 2022 redistricting, and she noted in an interview that “even after we no longer had overlapping geographical areas, we would frequently run into each other at reproductive rights events.” That makes her endorsement of Rogers “a complete reversal on her position,” Pohutsky continued. U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), tours the UA Local 333 training facility in Lansing, Mich. April 6, 2026 | Photo By Ben Solis/Michigan Advance An attempt was made by the Advance to contact Stevens for comment, but was unsuccessful. If a comment is received, this story will be updated. Her chief of staff resigned on Sunday after Stevens endorsed Rogers, and said many other staffers had also quit. Stevens has historically been an advocate for reproductive rights in her time as a legislator. A Planned Parenthood Action Fund endorsement page from her 2020 congressional campaign called her a “champion for reproductive health care.” She received a 100% score from Reproductive Freedom For All, and an “F” rating from anti-abortion group SBA Pro-Life America. And in a competitive 2022 primary following the U.S. Supreme Court decision to overturn Roe v. Wade, Stevens put her gender at the forefront of the race in her support of abortion rights. But now one of those same groups, Reproductive Freedom For All, is describing Stevens’ decision as “giving cover” to Rogers, a vocally and historically anti-abortion legislator. The group’s president and CEO, Mini Timmaraju, said in a statement criticizing Stevens “Nothing can erase Mike Rogers’ votes or make him any less dangerous to our reproductive freedom.” Rogers was condemned by Democrats for a radio interview with conservative Christian talk radio host Bob Dutko in October in which he pointed to his “100% pro-life rating” while previously in Congress, and assured Dutko that there was no concern that he would join Democrats on social issues in the Senate, including abortion rights. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE While Democratic Party leaders called it proof that Rogers would vote for a nationwide abortion ban, Rogers quickly pushed back on social media, reposting a video in which he said that when it comes to abortion, “Michigan voters have already decided the issue, and I respect that decision.” Though Michigan enshrined reproductive rights in its state constitution in 2022, many have warned that a constitutional convention — which is a ballot measure, Proposal One, in Tuesday’s election — could open the door to reversing that. “This is a battle that we are never going to have to stop fighting. I think that if we learned anything from the Dobbs decision, it’s that this is never going to be over,” Pohutsky said. “Just because we’ve enshrined it in our constitution, we can’t let our foot off the gas. Between Mike Rogers and Proposal 1 being on the ballot, there are existential threats to reproductive rights right now this election cycle, and I don’t think that’s going to change anytime soon.” On Stevens supporting Rogers and supporting abortion rights, Pohutsky said, “Those two things cannot exist in the same space.”

articles.title: The Mids: When to expect Michigan election results, and why they could take time
articles.description: Michigan began early tabulation for absentee ballots in 2024. But there are still times when election results are delayed in the hours, or even days, after polls have closed.
articles.content: Well, it’s happened, the Mids are here. Election Day, officially, is Tuesday, but judging by the crowd we saw at Michigan Public’s recent Issues & Ale event, many of you have already cast your ballots.Me? I’m old fashioned. I’ll be walking to my polling place tomorrow to stand in line with my neighbors and fill in the bubbles with a city-approved PaperMate Flair felt-tip pen like I’ve been doing for years.And then all that’ll be left to do is wait for the results to start trickling in. Speaking of which, we got this question, from Kara Gavin:Michigan began early tabulation for absentee ballots in 2024, which continued in this year’s primary. It may have played a role in getting results out more quickly, but the very close Democratic primary race for U.S. Senate was still too close to call the next morning.It did make me wonder: What’s going on with delayed election results in the hours, or even days, after polls have closed?“Never a good scenario,” said Muskegon City Clerk Ann Meisch, who walked me through the process.Meisch has been working elections for close to 35 years, and she’s seen some stuff.She said a big part of waiting on election results is that election workers have administrative work to do: validate ballot totals, seal bags and shut down precincts for the night.But if it’s 4 a.m. and results still aren’t in, it’s not a good sign.“That usually means that somebody is off somewhere,” Meisch said.How it's supposed to workBefore we go too far into the nightmare scenarios, let’s review what happens when everything goes right:1. Polls closeMost of the state’s polls close at 8 p.m.. A few places in the western U.P. stay open for another hour, because they’re in the Central Time Zone. But even when the polls close, anyone still in line is allowed to vote. And, any absentee ballots dropped by 8 p.m. still have to be collected.“So we have people that are like stationed there, and they’re off site,” Meisch said. “They’re looking at those. They’re bringing in any last minute absentee votes that they have, and then we’re going ahead and processing that.”2. Verify the ballot countThanks to the pre-processing, there’s probably not much tabulating going on at this point, just a small amount of last-minute ballots. Once all the ballots are fed into the machines, election workers check to make sure they have the right number of ballots cast.“So if I gave a precinct 500 ballots, they have to tell me what they did with their 500 ballots,” Meisch said.3. On the roadBest case scenario, the numbers match. Workers then print reports from the tabulators, scoop all the physical ballots from a bin in the machine, seal and deliver everything to the clerk’s office, where results are looked over again.“We pack everything up and then I have to drive to the county to hand-deliver all of our results,” Meisch said. “So they all are hand-delivered. They do not go through the internet or anything like that.”That last part is key to remember, if you find yourself getting impatient on election night. Vote totals have to travel physically to the clerk’s office. Electronic results are preserved on disk and delivered in person.If you see a truck late at night . . .At an election public accuracy test a few weeks ago in Grand Rapids, I ran into former Governor John Engler who now works with the Democracy Defense Foundation to help improve trust in elections.He said delivering results physically adds a safeguard to the election. But it also can make things take longer.“You get a big jurisdiction like Detroit, which is larger, and they’re coming in from all across the city, to a single counting place,” Engler said.As it gets later into the night, normal activity can sometimes be perceived as suspicious.“And then somebody will say, ‘Well, I saw a truck pull up,’” Engler said. “Well, if that truck is simply delivering the ballots from a particular precinct or five precincts, then there should be a truck.”Takeaway: before you post a video to TikTok alleging an election conspiracy, ask yourself, “Should there be a truck?”How it can go wrongIf all goes well, Meisch said results could come in by 11:30 or midnight. Here are reasons why results might arrive later:1. Ballot numbers don’t match upIf a polling place doesn’t have the same number of ballots as they do voters, workers have to go over everything again to find where the numbers went wrong.“So it could be going through all of the secrecy sleeves by hand and looking to see if a ballot was left in one of the secrecy sleeves,” Meisch said. “And I’ve got five workers down there all like going through all of them.”2. Abandoned ballotsMeisch told me there can be valid reasons the numbers don’t match: say a voter picks up a ballot, gets frustrated and leaves before casting the ballot. Poll workers are trained to note these incidents in a poll book, to help explain any discrepancies down the road.3. Ballots have to be retabulatedWith millions of votes being cast in hundreds of communities, mistakes can happen. Usually, if there are any issues, it’s not enough to sway the election. But not always. Just ask the mayor of Hamtramck.Meisch said if workers can’t resolve any discrepancy with the vote totals, the next step is to set the tabulator back to zero, take every ballot out of the bin below, and run them back through, one by one.So yeah, if it comes to that, it could be a while.“Know that we are working,” Meisch said. “We’re working really hard here.”What about trust?Kara’s original question asked how the speed of results reporting could affect trust in the outcome. We all remember the 2020 election, when absentee ballots weren’t processed until polls closed, and tabulation stretched for days while conspiracy theories spread online.But with absentee ballots now being processed earlier, the reality is any delay in reporting is likely because workers are trying extra hard to get the numbers right.“Counting votes is not a delay in the process, it is the process,” said Kent County clerk Lisa Posthumus Lyons. “But we want it to be transparent, and we want it to be as close to real time as possible.”That’s why she reports out Kent County results as they come into her office.“When I have results, I want our public to know what those results are,” Posthumus Lyons said. “So if I don’t have all of them, you’re going to see the results that we do have.”She doesn’t question that strategy even if it means one candidate is leading early in the evening, only to fall behind when more votes are reported.Other counties, including Muskegon County, take a different approach, waiting for all the votes to come in before releasing results to the public.Local clerks told me, in either case, they hear from their own community that they trust the results.“My residents, I think, have a lot of confidence and a lot of trust in us,” Meisch said.That trust even came through earlier this year, when President Trump named Muskegon in a speech over voter fraud. It was Meisch herself who discovered the alleged fraud and reported it.Still she heard about it from people outside of Muskegon.“The outside people, I can’t speak to them,” Meisch said. “I know that there’s different opinions and feelings about the election, and I definitely have heard from some of them as well.”When she does, she tries to explain the process, the work that goes into making sure ballots are secured, and that results are reported accurately.“You know there comes a point that I can’t fix how they feel,” she said. “But I do try.”Last chance to voteIf you plan to vote on election day, be sure to check in on all of our 2026 Midterm Election coverage. We’ve got interviews with candidates for governor, Secretary of State, Attorney General, Michigan Supreme Court and even a useful voter guide to the midterms..We’ll also have all the results as we get them at michiganpublic.org.Next time, we’ll wrap up The Mids with final takeaways from the election.Try to get some sleep,Dustin Dwyer, Reporter_______________________________Today’s newsletter was written by Dustin Dwyer, produced by Kalloli Bhatt, and edited by Michelle Keller.

Election administration and the 2020 election are hot topics in the Michigan gubernatorial race
articles.description: Jocelyn Benson has called John James an “election denier,” while the Republican has accused her of misrunning the state’s elections.
articles.content: This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access. This story also appeared in Votebeat When Michigan voters weigh in on who should be their next governor, they will be choosing between a man who said the state’s 2020 election process was “rigged and manipulated” and the woman who ran that election. It’s giving the race between U.S. Rep. John James, a Republican, and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, a Democrat, an interesting angle: Should a candidate’s stance on election administration dictate whether they can lead a state? Both campaigns appear to believe the answer is yes. Benson, who’s served as the state’s top election official since 2019, has named her work in that office as one of the key reasons voters should select her, saying in her candidate questionnaire for the Detroit Free Press that, under her stewardship, Michigan’s elections ranked “consistently among the top five.” (The Massachusetts Institute of Technology ranked Michigan’s elections in the top five in 2022 and 2024, and No. 7 in 2020.) Her campaign website boasts that Benson “oversaw two of the highest turnout and most transparent elections in the state’s history.” She’s regularly framed herself as an “election defender,” while James, she says, is an “election denier.” James said this summer that President Donald Trump won Michigan three times, even though President Joe Biden defeated him in the state in 2020. James and his campaign later said he was referring to Trump’s three wins in the state’s Republican primaries. James, in turn, has attacked Benson’s work on elections. In a podcast interview in June, James, who ran unsuccessfully for U.S. Senate in 2020, claimed without evidence that Benson “rigged and manipulated the election process to defeat me and President Trump.” James also signed onto a letter with other Michigan Republicans in Congress accusing Benson of allowing “an environment to persist where at least 15 non-citizens cast ballots” in the 2024 election. Michigan has charged a number of people since 2024 for voting despite not being U.S. citizens. Others are under investigation. Other Republicans have joined in. At a September press conference, for example, James joined with Jay DeBoyer (the GOP candidate for lieutenant governor) and Anthony Forlini (who is running to replace Benson as secretary of state) to attack Benson’s record as secretary. DeBoyer, who was the St. Clair County clerk before he became a state representative, said he used to tell his local clerks to not follow Benson’s election directives because they were in “direct violation of election law.” Forlini, who has served as Macomb County clerk since 2021, went after Benson’s handling of a spat between their respective offices in which he said he found a number of alleged noncitizens on the voter roll and Benson’s office warned other clerks against using the methodology Forlini used. While Forlini did find at least one noncitizen who had cast a ballot, further investigation found a number of the people he flagged were in fact citizens. If nothing else, voters are likely to walk away from the 2026 gubernatorial race more aware of what exactly a secretary of state’s role is, said Melissa R. Michelson, a professor of political science at Menlo College in California. It could also help encourage both parties to turn out, she said. Reminding Democrats that Benson ran contentious elections could excite them, Michelson said, while standing with Trump on his claims that the 2020 election was stolen is a standard way for Republican candidates to win the president’s backing. Trump has endorsed James in the gubernatorial race. James is “probably hoping that there’s a future for him, even if he doesn’t win this election,” Michelson said. “What better way to cement yourself as a loyal Republican who toes the party line and speaks Trump’s truth? Maybe that sets him up for something else in the future.” A poll conducted by Michigan State University political science professor Corwin Smidt found that 77% of likely voters in Michigan said they were at least somewhat confident their county would count their votes correctly. A lower number — 68% of likely voters — said they trusted the state as well. “The [Republican] rhetoric has not translated into a full erosion of trust down to 2020 levels,” Smidt said. After the 2020 election, he found that only 20% of Republicans said they were at least somewhat confident in statewide elections, per data he shared with Votebeat. That’s compared to more than 47% of Republicans in this latest survey ahead of the midterm. A few weeks before the election, he said the nearly 1,400 Michiganders surveyed were largely not concerned about election integrity, instead focusing on the cost of living and the economy at large. To Smidt, Republican claims about election fraud seem like more of a move to “solidify the base” rather than persuading voters concerned about the issue. But even if James loses, Michelson said his claims about Benson’s role in running the state’s elections could potentially set up future distrust. For one, it could affect voters’ views of this election, even though Benson has recused herself from the bulk of elections-related work. And beyond that, it could also color perceptions of future elections in the state more broadly. It’s a new playbook politicians have been using, Michelson said — elections are only fair if you’re the winner. “Every time a politician does this, it reduces public trust in elections,” she said. “It increases the difficulty of election officials doing their job. It increases the number of threats made. It makes it harder for election offices to get people to work at polling places because they don’t want to be confronted or intimidated or attacked.” Hayley Harding is a reporter for Votebeat based in Michigan. Contact Hayley at hharding@votebeat.org. Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization covering local election integrity and voting access. Sign up for their newsletters here.

articles.content: Find this story in your account’s ‘Saved for Later’ section. Halloween might be over, but the jump scares are not. This weekend, Mayor Zohran Mamdani stepped out for a few Halloweekend engagements with no beard, leaving in its stead a millennial mustache that has completely altered his appearance. Boo! Mamdani’s beard was last seen in this Día de Muertos video, which was posted Sunday — though it’s not clear when it was filmed. A representative from the mayor’s office confirmed to The Cut that Mamdani is participating in the age-old tradition known as Movember to “raise awareness around men’s health this month.” He is a millennial, after all. articles.title: Most of our measures of a key cognitive process don't agree
articles.description: A big study with very little beyond negative results still gets published.
articles.content: It's widely acknowledged that it's nearly impossible to publish negative results in scientific journals. "We didn't see anything" is a much harder sell than finding that a hypothesis is clearly right. Findings of no effect tend to either be shuffled off to low-profile journals or left behind as unpublished lab lore. The high-profile journal Nature, however, made a notable exception this week, publishing a study that tells us that a bunch of methods we have been using to try to measure a key emotional ability don't seem to be measuring the same thing. The results mean that we don't have a good way to measure the impact of a concept that is the basis of a key method in therapy. Inconsistencies One of the most successful forms of therapy is cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. In part, CBT is based on getting people to step back and engage in "cognitive reappraisal." This requires people to think over a situation that has caused a negative emotional response and find ways to reinterpret it so that it has less impact on them. The ability to engage in this process has been linked to emotional resilience.Read full article Comments

articles.content: Anthropic has updated Claude Code’s system prompt to prevent the AI tool from being used to re-create existing video games, as reported by Tom’s Hardware.
