El-Sayed, Michigan Democrats push to galvanize voters after stunning Senate race defection
articles.description: Michigan Democrats are scrambling to refocus voters' attention and move past a stunning defection in one of the nation’s most closely watched Senate races.
articles.content: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters during a campaign rally at Eastern Michigan University, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, in Ypsilanti, Mich.(Julia Demaree Nikhinson / AP)YPSILANTI, Mich. (AP) — Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and fellow Michigan Democrats scrambled on Monday to refocus attention on turning out voters for Election Day after his former primary rival stunned the party by endorsing the Republican candidate in one of the country’s most closely watched races.The final push before Tuesday's midterms followed a dramatic Sunday, when Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after appearing alongside him at church. It prompted her expulsion from the state Democratic Party and drew fierce condemnation from party leaders, including longtime allies.Speaking Monday morning at Eastern Michigan University, El-Sayed made no mention of the controversy, instead emphasizing that his campaign was about voters, not himself. Asked afterward what he would tell supporters nervous about the impact of Stevens’ endorsement on the race, El-Sayed had a simple message: “Go vote.”“There’s only one thing we can do to control the outcome,” he added. He was joined at Monday's rally by Sen. Elizabeth Warren and his grandparents, who greeted the crowd.With over 2.3 million Michigan voters having already cast their ballots as of Monday, the question is whether the extraordinary political drama will matter to those who have yet to vote. Nearly 4.5 million people voted in the 2022 midterms. The state’s regular early in-person voting period ended Sunday, with polls reopening statewide Tuesday.“Well, around half of people have already voted,” said Lori Goldman, a longtime Democratic organizer in Oakland County, a party stronghold near Detroit. “But for the rest, it could matter a hell of a lot.”Rogers, GOP tout Stevens' endorsementFor Rogers and Republicans, the endorsement represented a remarkable political coup. Rogers personally reached out to Stevens over the weekend, according to a person with direct knowledge of the discussions. Even Rogers’ own staff was unaware of the planned joint appearance at Perfecting Church until Sunday morning and learned of Stevens’ endorsement only when it was posted online, the person said. The campaign was touting the endorsement to voters Monday.For Democrats, the defection exposed lingering divisions over El-Sayed, who narrowly defeated Stevens in an expensive and bruising primary marked by disagreements over Israel and the war in Gaza. Party leaders had spent the final weeks of the campaign trying to shore up support for El-Sayed, particularly among Jewish and Black voters who had strongly backed Stevens.Those leaders — including some who have remained critical of their nominee — rebuked Stevens and said it would only energize their base. El-Sayed reported raising $2.4 million on Sunday, his largest fundraising day of the campaign, while the state party said it saw a surge of people volunteering to knock on doors.“I don’t think this changes the election results other than it galvanizes Democrats,” said Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel.Stevens is rebuked en masse by former supporters and critics alikeMichigan Democrats for months were divided on which candidate to support in the August primary, when El-Sayed defeated Stevens by around 14,000 votes.But in the weeks since, many have rallied around El-Sayed as the party’s nominee, and even those who haven’t expressed stunned anger at Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers.Adrian Hemond, a Democratic strategist who supported Stevens and has been so critical of El-Sayed that he plans to leave the Senate race blank, said the congresswoman’s endorsement had nothing to do with their policy differences: “If it did, she would have done it a month ago.”“This is colossally stupid. But it has zero to do with any substance. It has to do with personal animosity between these two,” Hemond said.Goldman, who supported Stevens in her first congressional campaign and has known her for a decade, said she was shocked by the reversal.“I think she’s thrown away a career that had import,” Goldman said. “I’m stunned. I’m stunned. And I feel a little heartbroken for her.”Debbie Rosenman, who leads two Democratic organizations in southeast Michigan, an area Stevens has partially represented in Congress for years, said the endorsement had left local Democrats feeling betrayed.“What I am hearing is fury,” Rosenman said. “They are just infuriated with her and feel betrayed by her.”Rosenman said the anger had also translated into increased volunteer activity, with people showing up at campaign offices without having signed up in advance. So many volunteers were seeking canvassing assignments, she said, that organizers had to move campaign literature between locations to meet demand.A timeline of the Democratic downfallSoon after her primary loss, Stevens endorsed El-Sayed, saying that she would do “whatever he wants me to do” on the campaign trail. But she remained absent from the campaign trail for months, something that became increasingly noticeable as Jewish leaders criticized El-Sayed.El-Sayed has been a vocal critic of Israel, and has been criticized for a statement in which he said “hurt people hurt people" after a synagogue attack and for appearing with controversial streamer Hasan Piker on the campaign trail.Those controversies largely preceded Stevens’ endorsement of El-Sayed. He has since apologized for his comments following the synagogue attack and has not appeared with Piker again. But Stevens and some Jewish leaders have maintained that he has not done enough to address their concerns. Her fiancé, Jason Turkish, said last week that he would vote for Rogers.The tensions came to a head over a planned Sunday unity event featuring Stevens and El-Sayed. After their public sparring over Israel and an outside group’s campaign advertisement threatened to overshadow the gathering, Rep. Debbie Dingell, a senior Michigan Democratic figure close to Stevens, said she uninvited the congresswoman because the dispute had become “distracting.”Dingell and other Democrats said Stevens had repeatedly reassured them throughout the week that the dispute would not cause her to withdraw her support for El-Sayed.Few anticipated what would happen Sunday morning, when Stevens walked into a Detroit church alongside Rogers and stood with him in the pews. She announced her endorsement of the Republican shortly afterward.“This is about Abdul getting angrier and angrier and saying, ‘I don’t want these people in my campaign,’” Stevens said later in a CNN interview. “This is a weight off my shoulders. I’m being straight with everybody.”Dingell, visibly shaken during a CNN interview afterward, called Stevens’ remarks “one of the most painful interviews I have watched” and said she had been worried about the congresswoman all week.

articles.title: Election integrity takes center stage in Michigan governor’s race
articles.description: Jocelyn Benson has called John James an “election denier,” while the Republican has accused her of misrunning the state’s elections.
articles.content: This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access. Sign up for Votebeat Michigan’s free newsletter here. When Michigan voters weigh in on who should be their next governor, they will be choosing between a man who said the state’s 2020 election process was “rigged and manipulated” and the woman who ran that election. It’s giving the race between U.S. Rep. John James, a Republican, and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, a Democrat, an interesting angle: Should a candidate’s stance on election administration dictate whether they can lead a state? Both campaigns appear to believe the answer is yes. Benson, who’s served as the state’s top election official since 2019, has named her work in that office as one of the key reasons voters should select her, saying in her candidate questionnaire for the Detroit Free Press that, under her stewardship, Michigan’s elections ranked “consistently among the top five.” (The Massachusetts Institute of Technology ranked Michigan’s elections in the top five in 2022 and 2024, and No. 7 in 2020.) Her campaign website boasts that Benson “oversaw two of the highest turnout and most transparent elections in the state’s history.” She’s regularly framed herself as an “election defender,” while James, she says, is an “election denier.” James said this summer that President Donald Trump won Michigan three times, even though President Joe Biden defeated him in the state in 2020. James and his campaign later said he was referring to Trump’s three wins in the state’s Republican primaries. Related: Jocelyn Benson vs. John James: What to know the Michigan governor’s race Fact checks: What’s true, false in Michigan governor’s race Benson, James both want change. Agreements end there Musk, Bloomberg help fuel late funding surge in governor’s race James, in turn, has attacked Benson’s work on elections. In a podcast interview in June, James, who ran unsuccessfully for U.S. Senate in 2020, claimed without evidence that Benson “rigged and manipulated the election process to defeat me and President Trump.” James also signed onto a letter with other Michigan Republicans in Congress accusing Benson of allowing “an environment to persist where at least 15 non-citizens cast ballots” in the 2024 election. Michigan has charged a number of people since 2024 for voting despite not being U.S. citizens. Others are under investigation. Other Republicans have joined in. At a September press conference, for example, James joined with Jay DeBoyer (the GOP candidate for lieutenant governor) and Anthony Forlini (who is running to replace Benson as secretary of state) to attack Benson’s record as secretary. DeBoyer, who was the St. Clair County clerk before he became a state representative, said he used to tell his local clerks to not follow Benson’s election directives because they were in “direct violation of election law.” Donate Forlini, who has served as Macomb County clerk since 2021, went after Benson’s handling of a spat between their respective offices in which he said he found a number of alleged noncitizens on the voter roll and Benson’s office warned other clerks against using the methodology Forlini used. While Forlini did find at least one noncitizen who had cast a ballot, further investigation found a number of the people he flagged were in fact citizens. If nothing else, voters are likely to walk away from the 2026 gubernatorial race more aware of what exactly a secretary of state’s role is, said Melissa R. Michelson, a professor of political science at Menlo College in California. It could also help encourage both parties to turn out, she said. Reminding Democrats that Benson ran contentious elections could excite them, Michelson said, while standing with Trump on his claims that the 2020 election was stolen is a standard way for Republican candidates to win the president’s backing. Trump has endorsed James in the gubernatorial race. James is “probably hoping that there’s a future for him, even if he doesn’t win this election,” Michelson said. “What better way to cement yourself as a loyal Republican who toes the party line and speaks Trump’s truth? Maybe that sets him up for something else in the future.” A poll conducted by Michigan State University political science professor Corwin Smidt found that 77% of likely voters in Michigan said they were at least somewhat confident their county would count their votes correctly. A lower number — 68% of likely voters — said they trusted the state as well. “The [Republican] rhetoric has not translated into a full erosion of trust down to 2020 levels,” Smidt said. After the 2020 election, he found that only 20% of Republicans said they were at least somewhat confident in statewide elections, per data he shared with Votebeat. That’s compared to more than 47% of Republicans in this latest survey ahead of the midterm. A few weeks before the election, he said the nearly 1,400 Michiganders surveyed were largely not concerned about election integrity, instead focusing on the cost of living and the economy at large. To Smidt, Republican claims about election fraud seem like more of a move to “solidify the base” rather than persuading voters concerned about the issue. But even if James loses, Michelson said his claims about Benson’s role in running the state’s elections could potentially set up future distrust. For one, it could affect voters’ views of this election, even though Benson has recused herself from the bulk of elections-related work. And beyond that, it could also color perceptions of future elections in the state more broadly. It’s a new playbook politicians have been using, Michelson said — elections are only fair if you’re the winner. “Every time a politician does this, it reduces public trust in elections,” she said. “It increases the difficulty of election officials doing their job. It increases the number of threats made. It makes it harder for election offices to get people to work at polling places because they don’t want to be confronted or intimidated or attacked.” Hayley Harding is a reporter for Votebeat based in Michigan. Contact Hayley at hharding@votebeat.org. Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization covering local election integrity and voting access. Sign up for their newsletters here.

Just last week we had a boiler go down that cost us about $36,000. How many more times can we repair it before it becomes obselete?” Easley said approving this bond proposals will better the entire neighborhood. “This is going to bring so much opportunity. Property value [will increase]. Strong school, strong community and strong property. A part of this plan will develope new STEAM spaces and career technical education spaces. There is extreme shortage in labor economy. articles.content: Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. We want researchers to challenge our assumptions and help strengthen both our systems and the methods we use to defend them. This is part of our ongoing effort to use AI to continuously find and fix weaknesses in our systems. Our last sprint showed what this approach can deliver. We dedicated 25% of our product engineers to finding and fixing weaknesses in our systems. Using Codex, engineers investigated findings, reproduced vulnerabilities in isolated environments and prepared patches for review. We’re building on that work because traditional cyber defenses alone are no longer sufficient. Recent incidents across the industry show how quickly threats can emerge and how important it is to build continuous defensive loops to find and fix weaknesses before attackers do. Keeping the defender’s window open requires organizations to use frontier cyber capabilities to harden their systems. We’re using our most capable models to strengthen our own defenses and making them available to Daybreak customers. We’ve committed $1 billion in subsidized access over six months for frontline defenders protecting essential services and digital infrastructure. We’re also sharing our architecture and lessons from the last sprint, alongside our blueprint for empowering cyber defenders across industry and government. We’ll keep advancing our models, using them to strengthen our own systems, and expanding access for trusted defenders. Keeping the defender’s window open will take action across the industry, and that work needs to start now.

articles.title: Rewarding defenders with bigger bug bounties
articles.description: OpenAI is raising Security Bug Bounty rewards and introducing report quality, loyalty, and priority campaign bonuses for independent security researchers.
articles.content: We’re raising rewards in OpenAI’s Security Bug Bounty program to further encourage independent researchers to pursue vulnerabilities in OpenAI software that our testing may have missed. We’re also introducing new incentives for researchers to earn more for higher quality vulnerability reports. Independent security researchers play an essential role in protecting technology across the industry. At OpenAI, incentivizing responsible disclosure is a core part of our security model, complementing our Defense Factory work, where our engineers use our models to find weaknesses, reproduce them, and test fixes. Today’s updates are designed to encourage and empower researchers, and to continue building a collaborative, community-first security environment. We’re more than quadrupling the midpoint of our reward ranges for medium, high, and critical findings on average. A critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000. Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses. The full details are available in our security bug bounty program(opens in a new window). High-quality reports will be eligible to earn a bonus multiplier on the base bounty. A reliable proof of concept that isolates the bug, shows when it can be exploited, and demonstrates its impact gives us a head start on a fix. The quality multiplier recognizes the extra work that makes a finding especially useful. To build long-term relationships and continuously empower our security community, we are introducing a tiered loyalty bonus program. This 5-tier system provides scaling bonuses to recognize, support, and celebrate researchers who consistently partner with us in making AI technology safer for everyone. To support community engagement as technology evolves, priority campaigns will feature dedicated bonus pools for newly launched features. These short-term campaigns give researchers early, high-reward opportunities to test new developments and be recognized for their early contributions. Medium - ChatGPT (core asset): A read-only member can upload files to a Project without write permission. $2,000 × 1.15 Quality Bonus × 1.05 Bronze Loyalty Tier Bonus High - Prism (non-core asset): IDOR resulting in reading a file uploaded to user’s Project $2,500 × 1.15 Quality Bonus × 1.10 Gold Loyalty Tier Bonus Critical - ChatGPT (core asset): One-click account takeover. $30,000 × 1.15 Quality Bonus × 1.30 Priority Campaign Bonus × 1.15 31337 Loyalty Tier Bonus Exceptional - ChatGPT (core asset): Significant compromise of a security boundary (e.g., ability to view arbitrary ChatGPT users’ chat messages.) $100,000 × 1.15 Quality × 1.30 Priority Campaign × 1.15 31337 loyalty All scenarios and historical awards are illustrative. If you’ve already submitted a report and we haven’t yet awarded a bounty, we’ll apply the new reward ranges. For bounties we awarded in the 30 days before this announcement, we’ll pay you the difference if your finding would have earned more under the new ranges (Base Award + Loyalty Awards). On November 20–21, our security team will be at PROMPT2PWN(opens in a new window) in Oakland, where researchers can test targets in person. If you’ll be there, we’d love to hear what you’ve been working on and how to partner with you. Thank you to everyone who has taken the time to investigate a lead and report it to us. We want OpenAI to be a team you come back to when you find something we’ve missed.

articles.description: The U.S. Department of Justice on Monday asked the U.S. Supreme Court to require California to set aside the ballots of suspected noncitizen voters in a last-ditch appeal by the Trump administration to exert control over the state’s vote counting. The request came on the eve of Election Day and as more than 5 million mail ballots have […]
articles.content: The U.S. Department of Justice logo is displayed on a speaker’s podium. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)The U.S. Department of Justice on Monday asked the U.S. Supreme Court to require California to set aside the ballots of suspected noncitizen voters in a last-ditch appeal by the Trump administration to exert control over the state’s vote counting. The request came on the eve of Election Day and as more than 5 million mail ballots have already been cast in California, a state where voters are expected to elect dozens of Democrats to the U.S. House. California’s election could be thrown into chaos if the Supreme Court grants the request. State and local election officials have previously warned that they have no easy way to quickly identify and set aside the ballots of individuals on the list. In the Trump administration’s emergency application, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer noted that federal law prohibits voting by noncitizens, who still do sometimes vote “despite that prohibition,” he wrote. “Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back,” Sauer added. Logistically difficult As a universal vote-by-mail state, every voter in California is sent a mail ballot. While millions of these ballots have already been returned, millions more may be dropped off on Tuesday or arrive by mail in the coming days. Aman Bhullar, an assistant Los Angeles County registrar-recorder/county clerk, warned in a court declaration in October that the Trump administration’s request could wreak havoc on elections. “The potential consequences of implementing DOJ’s demand are severe and range from halting all counting; halting in-person voters’ ability to cast votes; or otherwise interfering with the ability to accurately count votes,” Bhullar wrote. Already a week ago, Shelby Wayment, staff attorney at the University of California, Los Angeles Safeguarding Democracy Project, questioned the feasibility of the DOJ’s demands. Ballots have already been mailed out and were being processed, she said. “Just logistically, I don’t think it’s possible at this point,” Wayment said in a late October interview. No widespread fraud The Justice Department sued California in October, alleging that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security had identified 20,000 suspected noncitizen voters. California officials raised concerns about the veracity of the list, and declined to take action based on it. An immigrant rights group, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, has raised serious concerns about the list after a judge forced the Trump administration to share a copy with the organization. The group said in a court filing Saturday that an analysis by data experts found that 42% of the names weren’t found on California’s current voter file. At least 22 names on the list match names of U.S. citizens compiled by the organization, the analysis found. “There is no widespread voter fraud. The federal government has no right to interfere in California’s elections,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said in a statement on Saturday. 11th hour challenge The Justice Department has said the Department of Homeland Security compiled the list by checking a public copy of California’s voter file against federal records and information from the research service Lexis Nexis. A district court judge and the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals have both ruled against the Trump administration in the case. State and local officials have argued the Justice Department exceeded its authority because states administer elections under the U.S. Constitution. Even though the 9th Circuit issued a decision on Friday, the Justice Department didn’t ask the Supreme Court to intervene until midday Monday, less than 24 hours before Election Day. The Justice Department has asked for an administrative stay that would require California to begin segregating ballots of voters on the list while the Trump administration prepares a full appeal. While it’s unknown how the Supreme Court will rule, in general the justices frown on federal courts ordering major last-minute changes to elections. Because the case arises out of the 9th Circuit, Justice Elena Kagan, one of the court’s three liberals, will be the first to review the application. Walter Olsen, a senior fellow at the Cato Institute’s Robert A. Levy Center for Constitutional Studies, in a statement predicted the Supreme Court will reject the request. He argued that the Justice Department is asking California officials to violate their own state laws. “The Supreme Court should and I believe will reject the administration’s nervy last-minute attempts to meddle in California’s elections, as lower courts have rejected them,” Olsen said.

Energy costs dominate midterms; climate battles play out down ballot
articles.description: This story was originally published by Capital & Main. In the final stretch of the 2026 midterm campaigns, the most potent climate issue in American politics arrived by delivery truck across the country. The average price of heating oil hit $6.23 a gallon for the week of Oct. 26, up from $3.60 a year earlier, […]
articles.content: Diesel fuel at this Ann arbor, Michigan gas station was selling for $7.39 a gallon on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)This story was originally published by Capital & Main. In the final stretch of the 2026 midterm campaigns, the most potent climate issue in American politics arrived by delivery truck across the country. The average price of heating oil hit $6.23 a gallon for the week of Oct. 26, up from $3.60 a year earlier, according to the Energy Information Administration. At that price, filling a 250-gallon tank cost about $1,557 — roughly $657 more than the year before. As cold weather settled over the Northeast, Democrats turned that bill into an attack on Republican candidates. In New Hampshire, where about 43% of residents heat with oil, Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Chris Pappas said energy costs and heating oil prices were “the beginning and end of every conversation I’m having on the campaign trail.” That is the pattern across the closest races in this cycle. Energy is everywhere on the ballot — as heating oil, diesel, power bills and water — but almost always as a question of price. The argument over what actually powers the country — fossil fuels or renewables — surfaces mostly down-ballot, in low-profile contests for the commissions that regulate utilities and drilling. “If you talk to voters, they are upset about their energy bills and they’re upset about data centers,” Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet, which backs climate-focused candidates in state and local races, told Capital & Main. “People want to hear from politicians about their plans on their energy bills and their plans on their data centers.” The consequences reach far beyond any one state. Control of the Senate will determine whether Congress revisits the clean energy tax credits Republicans rolled back in last year’s budget law. And the governors and regulators elected Tuesday will approve the gas plants, transmission lines and data center deals that shape the grid for decades to come. The U.S. Senate More than $191 million was spent on political ads referencing utility and energy bills in the first nine months of 2026, plus another $96.3 million from Oct. 1 to Oct. 16, according to AdImpact data analyzed by Climate Power, a Democratic-aligned advocacy group. In Maine, heating oil defined the final weeks of the race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democrat challenger Troy Jackson. Jackson said Mainers were paying 80% more for heating oil than a year earlier. Collins countered with an announcement: a release of 315,000 barrels from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, which she and her counterpart, Sen. Angus King, had requested of President Donald Trump. Climate itself registers here, too: In the Environmental Voter Project’s polling of eight U.S. Senate battlegrounds, Maine had the highest share of voters naming it a top-three priority at 22%. In the farm belt, the price that matters is the cost of diesel. In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek released a closing ad on fuel prices against Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson. Both candidates said data centers shouldn’t receive tax breaks — in a state that already gets more than 60% of its power from wind and solar. Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, yet Adam Hamilton built his challenge to Republican Sen. Roger Marshall around energy and utility costs, while Marshall said Kansans were “on fire” over data centers. High fuel and fertilizer prices have strained the farm economy in a state that generates roughly 50% of its electricity from wind. Data centers have scrambled the usual partisan lines. In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown branded Republican Sen. Jon Husted “the face of data centers,” and WinSenate, the country’s main Democratic Senate super PAC, ran an ad implying corrupt dealings between Husted and an energy company, though Husted was never charged. Kelcy Warren, executive chairman of the pipeline giant Energy Transfer, gave $3,500 to Husted’s campaign in late September. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers agree on little except data centers: Both back moratoriums in some form. El-Sayed’s framework would bar utilities from using data center demand to weaken Michigan’s clean-energy laws, while Rogers holds up to $250,000 in a Blackstone real estate trust that backs data centers. The climate stakes are concrete: Surging data center demand could trigger a provision in the state’s climate law that lets fossil fuel plants stay online during a capacity shortage. In Texas, where Democratic state Rep. James Talarico faces Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton for a critical U.S. Senate seat, the backdrop is Gov. Greg Abbott’s audit of every data center seeking to connect to the ERCOT grid — a review that won’t be finished until December, long after the midterm votes are cast. In Alaska, the fossil fuel question barely registers. Both Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola support oil and gas expansion, so the fight is over who will deliver it and who is to blame for Iran war-driven fuel costs. Sullivan has made the Alaska LNG pipeline, backed by a $54 billion South Korean investment, a centerpiece of his campaign. The Statehouses Thirty-six states will elect governors this November, and the nonpartisan Cook Political Report considers 12 of those contests competitive — including Alaska, Iowa, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, Florida and Texas, where Republicans now hold the office. In 39 states, utility regulators are appointed by governors or legislatures rather than elected — which means many of those governors become energy policymakers whether they campaign on it or not. Climate surfaces more openly in Alaska’s overlooked governor’s race, where Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has pressed the state to address climate change and said it relies too heavily on natural gas — rare talk from an Alaska politician. Republicans Dave Bronson, Treg Taylor and Bernadette Wilson are also on the ballot. Nathaniel Stinnett, founder of the Environmental Voter Project, called Kreiss-Tomkins “probably the favorite” but said the race is “extraordinarily close.” In the group’s polling, 21% of likely Alaska voters identified climate as a top-three priority, second only to Maine. “I don’t wanna pretend like this is a climate election,” Stinnett said. “But certainly thousands and perhaps tens of thousands of Alaskans are going to vote with climate change top of mind.” In Nevada, the main climate focus is water. Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo sued the Trump administration over cuts to the state’s allotment of water from the Colorado River, and Arizona has since joined the suit. Nevada Conservation Voters gave Lombardo a C+ grade, crediting his support of clean energy while faulting his backing of fossil fuel projects. Because Democrats already control both chambers of the legislature, a win by his challenger, Attorney General Aaron Ford, would give the party a trifecta. Stinnett noted that Ford has talked up the clean energy transition in a state that “is kind of like the Saudi Arabia of solar energy, or it can be.” Kansas offers Republicans their best chance to flip a Democratic-held governorship. Republican Ty Masterson is more moderate on energy than many in his party, and both he and Democrat Cindy Holscher voted for a 2025 data center tax exemption. Holscher has since said she would freeze data center development until stronger guardrails are in place. Georgia’s open governor’s race between Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson will shape the state’s energy direction too — but the most direct fight over Georgia’s power sits further down the ballot. Legislatures may matter as much. Spears, the Climate Cabinet director, is focused on five states where Democrats could win full control — Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania. “If they were a country, they’d be the world’s ninth largest climate polluter,” she said. “But 22 flipped seats stand between five trifectas and none.” Minnesota and Michigan both passed 100% clean energy laws the last time Democrats held full control. In Pennsylvania, where Republicans control the state Senate but not the House, Spears was blunt: “The Pennsylvania State Senate is where clean energy bills go to die.” The Regulators This is where fossil fuels and renewables actually collide. Spears called these “weird statewides” and said that as utility bills have become a defining issue, the culture war is “getting involved in utility elections as well.” Control of the Georgia Public Service Commission, which oversees Georgia Power, is on the ballot. Democrat Peter Hubbard, who won a special election last year, faces a rematch with Republican Fitz Johnson, while Republican Josh Tolbert and Democrat Shelia Edwards vie for an open seat. Republicans hold a 3-2 majority; if both Democrats win, Georgia would join Illinois’ commission as the nation’s only ones that are Democratic aligned. Hubbard argued the state is “oversubscribed on fossil fuels.” Johnson said data centers will pay their fair share because of protections he put in place. In Texas, the race for the Railroad Commission — which, despite its name, regulates an oil and gas industry that supplied nearly half the country’s oil last year — tightened after Republican Bo French drew widespread condemnation for a racist post on X. The Texas Oil and Gas Association, which represents ExxonMobil and Chevron, left him off its latest endorsement list. French has been bankrolled largely through PACs funded by billionaires Tim Dunn and Farris Wilks. His opponent, Democratic state Rep. Jon Rosenthal, is a former oil-field mechanical engineer. A Democrat hasn’t held a seat on the commission since 1994. Rosenthal traced the split to a rule backed by Jim Wright, the incumbent French ousted in the Republican primary, requiring liners for shallow oilfield waste pits so they don’t “leak noxious poison into the surrounding land and water, which I think most people think is a reasonable precaution.” Rosenthal, who said he has taken almost no money from oil and gas operators, has proposed banning industry donations to commissioners. “If we actually had ethical campaign finance laws, you wouldn’t want these people’s campaigns to be wholly or majorly funded by the people they’re supposed to regulate,” he said. “But that’s just how it is in Texas.” French did not respond to Capital & Main’s request for comment. In Arizona, Republicans Kevin Thompson and Ralph Heap face Democrats Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill for two seats on the Corporation Commission as electricity provider the Arizona Public Service seeks a roughly 14% rate increase — and the decision is not expected until after the election. Heap’s platform, endorsed by right wing group Turning Point, reportedly centers on prioritizing coal. Even if both Democrats win, Republicans keep a majority, since only two of five seats are up. Colorado voters face the most literal version of the question. Amendment 82 would add a right to buy and sell natural gas to the state constitution and could limit state and local governments’ ability to enforce natural gas regulations. It needs 55% of the vote to pass. It is one of eight measures funded by the conservative group Advance Colorado — and the state’s own oil and gas industry opposed it, wary of upsetting its 2024 truce with Gov. Jared Polis. Voters make governors, utility regulators answer for high power bills
articles.description: As broad affordability concerns define elections across the country, voters in several states on Tuesday will have a say on their future utility bills. State utility regulators, who are facing heightened levels of attention and scrutiny amid high prices, are on the ballot in nine states: Alabama, Arizona, Georgia, Louisiana, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma […]
articles.content: A group of Maine residents protest a proposed electricity price increase ahead of an October 2025 public hearing in Freeport. Rising utility prices are increasingly drawing scrutiny from voters and state officials. (Photo by AnnMarie Hilton/Maine Morning Star)As broad affordability concerns define elections across the country, voters in several states on Tuesday will have a say on their future utility bills. State utility regulators, who are facing heightened levels of attention and scrutiny amid high prices, are on the ballot in nine states: Alabama, Arizona, Georgia, Louisiana, Montana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma and South Dakota. Most Americans are served by utilities overseen by state regulators, who approve or deny rate increase requests from providers. Public outcry over rising utility prices has pushed state regulators and lawmakers to consider rate freezes, additional energy assistance funds or new rates targeting large energy users such as data centers. And it’s brought even more attention to high prices in races for both governors and utility regulators. “I think it’s different and it really emerged in the off-year elections,” said Ted Thomas, an energy consultant and the former Republican chair of the Arkansas Public Service Commission. “It began to emerge in 2024 as part of the overall concern on inflation, and then it seemed to have gone beyond that with a focus on energy specifically.” Utility prices played a major role in 2025 Democratic gubernatorial wins in New Jersey and Virginia. And in Georgia, Democrats last year flipped two seats on the board that regulates public utilities — the first time Democrats won statewide constitutional office there in nearly two decades. Thomas is a senior adviser to the consumer advocacy group PowerLines, which is tracking how gubernatorial and utility regulator candidates are talking about power bills in races across the country. This cycle has so far proven bruising for incumbent utility regulators: In Alabama, two Republican incumbents were ousted during primary and runoff elections as the state faces some of the highest electricity prices in the South. Two of the three Alabama Public Service Commission seats are on the ballot Tuesday. Likewise, in Arizona, a Republican incumbent lost during his primary contest, leaving two Democrats and two Republicans running for two open seats this week. The Arizona Corporation Commission is currently composed of five Republicans. “We can literally elect folks that are going to lower our electricity bills,” state Rep. Mariana Sandoval, a Democrat, said last month, according to the Arizona Mirror. While Thomas expects an anti-incumbency wave Tuesday, he noted that there’s no guarantee for immediate relief on consumers’ bills. Though lawmakers of both parties are increasingly scrutinizing high electricity prices, state leaders say they have little ability to lower costs because of broader energy market realities. While states can’t stop rising prices altogether, Thomas said they can do more to protect consumer pocketbooks and ensure residential households aren’t paying for large-scale industrial energy users. “It’s a large, complex system that costs a lot of money, and it provides an essential service that is a good value, even at an elevated price,” he said. “But at the same time, (affordability) needs to be more of a priority. It doesn’t need to be the back burner issue.” Utilities have requested billions of dollars in upcoming rate increases across the country. This winter, U.S. households are projected to spend an average of $1,030 to heat their homes, an increase of $82 over last year, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association. That organization, which represents state employees administering federal energy assistance programs, said this winter’s predicted 8.7% increase is more than 2.5 times the rate of inflation. Projections are more daunting for the large share of people in Northeastern states who heat their homes with oil. The association projects a 50% spike in the average cost of heating homes with oil this winter. The LCV Victory Fund, a political action committee associated with the League of Conservation Voters, has pledged to spend over $110 million to help elect Democrats to key House, Senate, and state races. Since summer, that organization has targeted the “energy bill voter,” which it describes as a crucial voting bloc of women, Black and Latino people, non-college-educated residents and voters who are less engaged with politics. “This is an energy election,” Sara Schreiber, senior vice president of campaigns at LCV Victory Fund, said in an October news release. “We identified early on that Republicans were vulnerable when it came to energy costs. Voters are not simply frustrated, they’re angry at monopoly utility companies, Big Tech, and Big Oil, who are making record profits while families struggle.” While much of the backlash over rising costs has focused on the growing number of data centers, electricity providers say that isn’t the major driver of rising prices. In a recent study it commissioned, the Edison Electric Institute, which represents the nation’s investor-owned electric utilities, said electric providers were working with state regulators to ensure data centers pay their fair share “and help keep electricity as affordable as possible.” That study blamed rising prices on higher wholesale electricity prices and broader issues with regional multistate grids — components of electric bills that are not controlled by electric companies or state regulators. “Our focus is on protecting existing customers and communities and strengthening the grid we all rely on,” Edison Electric Institute President and CEO Drew Maloney said in a news release last month. Stateline reporter Kevin Hardy can be reached at khardy@stateline.org. articles.content: Protestors gather at the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin, Michigan on Nov. 1, 2026, for a Day of the Dead ceremony to honor those who have died in ICE custody. (Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz/Michigan Advance)The day was coming to an end, and the GEO sign identifying the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin remained covered with photographs of people who had died while in the hands of immigration enforcement. An offering of flower petals, bread, drinks and candles reflected El Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, an Indigenous-rooted tradition observed Oct. 31-Nov. 2 in parts of Latin America, particularly Mexico, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia, to honor the dead. Organized by several Immigrant Rights advocates from Muskegon to Detroit, approximately 100 people from across the state gathered outside North Lake, the largest ICE detention center in the Midwest, to honor and remember those who have died in ICE custody, as well as those killed by ICE and Border Patrol agents this year. They were also standing in solidarity with those held inside the processing center operated by the Florida-based private contractor GEO Group. “The purpose of this event is to amplify the names of those who have been brutally taken from their families, their loved ones, their community by ICE or CBP,” Ale Rojas with Movimiento Cosecha and No Detention Centers in Michigan, told Michigan Advance. “One of the biggest things for us right now is recognizing that we, as a community, are hurting, so we can continue to build community and remember that we can show up for each other.” Flyers hang on the GEO Group sign at the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin, Michigan on Nov. 1, 2026, in remembrance of individuals who have died in ICE custody or whose death were connected to immigration enforcement. (Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz/Michigan Advance) Bringing together so many activist organizations and coalitions from across Michigan was easier than it had been a few months ago, Rojas said, noting that “the desire for action, for an actual movement, seems to be stronger now among organizations throughout the state.” No Detention Centers in Michigan; Movimiento Cosecha GR; West Michigan Clergy Action; the Coalition to Shut the Camps; Asamblea Popular Detroit; and Metro Detroit DSA were among the organizers. The number of fatalities linked to immigration enforcement across the country has increased compared to previous years. Since the beginning of Donald Trump’s second administration, at least 57 deaths have been recorded in ICE custody, including the death of Nenko Gantchev, a Bulgarian citizen and Chicago resident, which occurred last December in North Lake, along with at least 11 fatal shootings involving ICE and Border Patrol agents. The most recent person to be fatally shot by immigration agents was Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 26-year-old Colombian national who died July 13 in Biddeford, Maine, during an ICE operation. The most recent individual to die while in custody was Guillermo Pascual Verganza, a 43-year-old Guatemalan citizen who passed away Oct. 24 at the Otay Mesa detention center in San Diego, California. In Michigan, the most recent case of a death linked to an immigration operation involves Mario David Coronado Juárez, 35, a Guatemalan man who died Sept. 20 in a traffic accident in Grand Rapids in which ICE was involved. articles.content: As part of One Health Week, the World Health Organization (WHO) One Health Initiative is convening a webinar highlighting how a One Health approach can strengthen prevention and address health risks at the human–animal–environment interface. Prevention is a key priority in WHO’s global strategy, including through the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (GPW14), which highlights prevention, action on health determinants and response to climate-related health risks. Recent global health instruments, including the 2024 amendments to the International Health Regulations and the WHO Pandemic Agreement, further reinforce the importance of coordinated action across sectors for prevention, preparedness and response. The webinar will showcase WHO’s technical work to advance prevention through a One Health approach, including efforts to eliminate dog-mediated human rabies, strengthen integrated surveillance and information-sharing across human, animal and environmental health, advance prevention of emerging and infectious disease risks, and address climate-related health risks through the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health (ATACH). Speakers will share practical examples of how multisectoral approaches can help identify and address risks at their source, support coordinated and cost-effective action, and deliver public health benefits. A moderated discussion will explore how these approaches work in practice, the conditions needed to sustain and scale them, and opportunities for continued collaboration across sectors. The presentations will be followed by a moderated discussion with the speakers, focusing on how prevention through a One Health approach can be strengthened and applied across different contexts. articles.title: How are synthetic voices created for natural speech?
articles.description: Learn how synthetic voices are created, from speech data to neural text to speech, plus voice cloning, voice design, and how to spot an AI voice.
articles.content: Introducing Eleven v4Meet Eleven v4, our most emotive model yet. Today’s sophisticated AI models create synthetic voices that sound like natural speech. Trained on huge datasets of real human voices, these models use advanced neural networks to identify and replicate authentic speech patterns. Creating a synthetic voice is also called speech synthesis or voice synthesis, while the audio it produces is called synthetic speech. To create a new synthetic voice, a user records themselves talking. Meanwhile, the AI model analyzes their unique phonetic patterns and inflection and uses this data to replicate their voice. Then, the user can adjust vocal characteristics like accent, tone, and pacing to create the final product. Some synthetic voices are a direct clone of one person’s speech, while others are a blend of multiple voices. Voices can also be designed from a text description, with no recording at all. Synthetic voices open up a wide range of creative possibilities for podcasts, audiobooks, video games, and advertising. In this article, we’ll explore how synthetic voices are created, what makes them sound natural, and how to build your own synthetic voice with ElevenLabs. Create your Instant Voice Clone with ElevenCreative Synthetic voice creation is a three-step process. Here’s what that looks like in practice: Neural text to speech models are trained on numerous datasets of real speech recordings. This dataset includes recordings with different languages, accents, emotions, and pitch levels. Neural text to speech is a widely used form of speech synthesis today. Traditional models stitched together existing recordings of words, syllables, and phonemes. The results were very robotic, as they couldn’t replicate the variations in pitch, rhythm, and expression that make speech sound human. Instead of just learning how letters and syllables sound, modern neural text to speech models learn natural human pronunciation patterns and speech rhythms. When converting text to speech, these models assess the text, convert it into acoustic features, then use those features to generate waveforms. Since acoustic features like pitch, rhythm, and tone are built into neural AI models, the resulting speech sounds much more natural and authentic than the models of the past. The results are also customizable: you can change factors like speed, emotion, and even accent to get the exact voice you’re looking for. For example, your brand could use the same synthetic voice across your website but use excitement and urgency for marketing content and calmness for customer service interactions. Text to speech models fall into three broad generations. Understanding the differences between them helps contextualize why modern models, like ElevenLabs Text to Speech, can sound so natural. Modern voice platforms rely on neural and generative models, while standard text to speech mostly survives in legacy systems. Synthetic voices generated by AI sound very similar to human voices. In fact, it can be challenging to tell the difference between them if you’re not listening closely. There are two reasons why AI-generated voices sound more natural than the robotic voices of the past: prosody and context awareness. Prosody is the rhythm of natural human speech. Small changes in intonation and speed convey tone and emotion as we talk. For example, speaking quickly might convey stress or excitement, while raising your pitch at the end of a sentence turns a statement into a question. Today’s AI voice models are trained to understand and replicate prosody. This means the output reflects the flow of natural human conversation, rather than sounding stiff or flat. If you’re using a synthetic voice to narrate an audiobook or create video game dialogue, it will use prosody to reflect the character’s emotions. If you’re creating an educational content voiceover or customer service AI agent, the AI model will adjust the prosody for calm, empathetic delivery. By understanding prosody, AI models can also replicate unique accents. For example, the rhythm of a North American English accent sounds very different from a British, Scottish, or Irish English accent, even though they’re speaking the same language. Instead of processing each word individually, AI-powered TTS models assess the entire phrase, sentence, or conversation and adjust delivery based on the context. For example, there are many words that are spelled the same but are pronounced differently depending on the tense and context. For example, the word “read” is pronounced like “reed” in the present tense but pronounced like “red” in the past tense. Since AI voices are context-aware, they identify the appropriate pronunciation based on the rest of the text. They also adjust their delivery so the tone and emotion are appropriate for the situation. Voice cloning works by using AI to assess a real person’s voice, then applying their vocal characteristics to synthetic speech. First, the person cloning their voice must provide a short audio sample. The AI model uses the audio sample to identify the person’s accent, pitch, tone, and cadence. The model uses these characteristics to create a digital replica of the person’s voice. Users can generate new speech in this voice using text to speech technology. There are two types of voice cloning: Instant and Professional. Instant cloning creates a voice replica with less than two minutes of sample audio. This makes it easy to test voice options before committing to a larger project. Professional cloning uses between 30 minutes and three hours of audio samples to create a high-fidelity voice clone. Professional Voice Clones preserve subtle details like emotion and intonation that aren’t present in Instant Clones. They also require identity verification. Voice cloning has a variety of use cases, from generating voiceovers quickly to preserving voices that might otherwise be lost. The quality of a voice clone depends on the quality of the recording. Even without expensive recording equipment, there are a lot of small things you can do to improve how your voice clone sounds. These habits help you capture clean samples: While Instant Cloning needs less audio and Professional Cloning needs more, both depend on clean recordings. Clean audio of the right length gives better results than a large amount of noisy audio. Not every synthetic voice starts with a recording. With Voice Design, you describe the voice you want in text, including details like age, gender, accent, tone, and pacing, and the AI model generates voice options that match your description. You can listen to the options, choose the one you like, and save it to your voice library. Voice Design is useful when you need a voice for a character, a brand, or a product and there is no real person to clone. Read the Voice Design documentation to learn how to write effective voice descriptions. There is no single giveaway that proves a voice is AI-generated. Combining careful listening, detection tools, and a check on where the audio came from works better than relying on any one of them. Many people think they can tell the difference between a real voice and an AI-generated one, but they don’t always get it right. articles.title: Rep. Haley Stevens endorses Abdul El-Sayed's GOP challenger in Michigan race
articles.content: After losing the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, Congresswoman Haley Stevens revoked her endorsement of him Sunday and threw her support behind his Republican opponent. A MARTÍNEZ, HOST: A despicable betrayal. That is how Democratic Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is describing the 11th-hour drama unfolding in the critical Michigan U.S. Senate race.LEILA FADEL, HOST: Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary to Abdul El-Sayed, says she's revoking her endorsement of him and backing his GOP opponent. In a moment, we'll discuss all this with Michigan Democratic Congresswoman Debbie Dingell. We begin with the news.MARTÍNEZ: NPR congressional reporter Sam Gringlas has been tracking the story from Michigan, joins us now from Ann Arbor. So, Sam, I mean, this is the question I think everyone has on their mind - why is this happening now with just a few hours left in the campaign?SAM GRINGLAS, BYLINE: Yeah. Yeah. So, A, we talk about October surprises in campaigns. You don't often get a November surprise, which is exactly what we have here. Stevens endorsed El-Sayed after losing the primary by about a percentage point, but aside from a unity event right after that, they never campaigned together. And in recent days, Stevens started ramping up criticism of El-Sayed.The two Democrats traded seething statements. An attempted unity appearance for a Sunday Souls to the Polls event was scheduled at a church in Detroit and then fell apart. And instead of attending that event on Sunday with El-Sayed, she showed up at another Detroit church with his GOP opponent, Mike Rogers.MARTÍNEZ: Yeah. So how is Stevens explaining her reversal?GRINGLAS: Stevens emerged from that service with Rogers by her side and told reporters her endorsement was a personal decision.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)HALEY STEVENS: I'm not trying to harm anyone. I worked really hard for Democrats. I'm not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote. When you see repeated hate, it's not acceptable. I still love the party. Everyone should be fired up for Democrats.GRINGLAS: El-Sayed has made comments around Israel that have unsettled some Jewish voters. He's a vocal critic. She's a staunch defender. Stevens says El-Sayed did not do enough to reassure these voters or to disavow rhetoric made by some of his supporters she says is dangerous. But up to the last minute, multiple Democrats have said publicly that Stevens was affirming to them she was still backing El-Sayed.And, you know, as we talk about campaign rhetoric, I should also note the Rogers' campaign has focused its closing argument trying to paint El-Sayed, who'd be the first Muslim U.S. senator, as un-American.MARTÍNEZ: What has El-Sayed had to say?GRINGLAS: I was at the Detroit Church El-Sayed and Stevens had been slated to attend together, and El-Sayed told reporters there he does not think about Haley Stevens at all.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)ABDUL EL-SAYED: None of this matters. You know what matters? You can go, like, 15 minutes that way or 15 minutes that way and there are families who are preparing to send their kids to schools tomorrow that look like they did 50 years ago. They're worried about what they're going to feed their kids for lunch.GRINGLAS: I have met Democrats who did not support El-Sayed in the primary and struggled with their vote this fall. Now, will this latest drama sway a bunch of late deciders? Maybe not. Still, this cannot be the closing discussion El-Sayed's campaign was hoping for.MARTÍNEZ: Now how are other Democrats, then, responding to the situation?GRINGLAS: Holding this seat is key to Democrats retaking the Senate. A lot of them are fuming and have rallied around El-Sayed. Stevens' longtime chief of staff announced he and many staff have now quit, saying they're shocked and heartbroken by her actions. And the Michigan Democratic Party chair wrote that Stevens was no longer a member.MARTÍNEZ: So this matters because the Senate majority is on the line, but do you think this episode will reverberate beyond Tuesday in any way?GRINGLAS: This turmoil re-exposed fault lines within the party that have been deepening all year, not just over Israel, but about the party's identity going forward. Even if Democrats reclaim one or both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, that won't resolve these questions. So this debate is going to continue, especially as Democrats prepare to choose a presidential nominee in 2028. One of the earliest primary states to weigh in will be Michigan.MARTÍNEZ: That is NPR congressional reporter Sam Gringlas. Thanks a lot, Sam.GRINGLAS: You're welcome. Copyright © 2026 NPR. articles.title: Belgian prime minister quits after budget talks fail as king mulls whether to accept his resignation
articles.description: Belgian prime minister quits after budget talks fail as king mulls whether to accept his resignation AP News Belgium Needs Deeper Budget Cuts to Stabilize Debt, OECD Says Bloomberg Belgian government in crisis after budget talks collapse Reuters Belgium's king considering PM's resignation, palace says Euronews.com Belgian PM Who Blocked Ukraine’s Russian Assets Loan Offers Resignation Kyiv Post
articles.content: BRUSSELS (AP) — Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever handed in his resignation on Monday as a long-simmering budget crisis boiled over, but King Philippe has not yet decided whether to accept it. De Wever, a conservative Flemish nationalist, took office determined to tackle heavily indebted Belgium’s budget problems but failed to win the support of the other members of his five-party government for his proposals. Belgium’s Royal Palace confirmed that De Wever had resigned “following the failure of budget negotiations within his government.” The King, who oversees the formation of national governments, is “withholding his decision” on whether to approve. “The King regrets the lack of an agreement that would provide the country with a credible budget capable of addressing the challenges it currently faces,” said a statement from the palace, following a meeting of about an hour between the two men. King Philippe intends to consult with party group leaders from Tuesday, before receiving De Wever at the palace again on Friday. De Wever, who took office in February 2025, is now struggling to clinch a deal on the 2027 budget before Dec. 31. Belgium is one of the most heavily indebted countries in the 27-nation European Union, along with France and Italy. Its debt load has been mounting for years, but the COVID pandemic and an energy crisis made things worse. The European Commission has forecast Belgium’s debt to rise to 110% of its gross domestic product this year. The interest accumulating on that debt also poses a major challenge at a time when the government wants to boost defense spending. The government crisis comes against a backdrop of growing student protests in the country and frequent strikes, including several “national action days” led by unions.

articles.title: Michigan Democrats rally behind El-Sayed as Stevens goes rogue to support Rogers
articles.description: DETROIT — Key Democrats said Sunday they would not let Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers divide the party ahead of Tuesday’s election. Stevens, a sitting member of Congress, was all but formally exorcized by her party after she publicly endorsed Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, whom she […]
articles.content: U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina), center left, speaks during a press conference supporting U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, center right, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 at North End Church of God in Christ in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)DETROIT — Key Democrats said Sunday they would not let Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers divide the party ahead of Tuesday’s election. Stevens, a sitting member of Congress, was all but formally exorcized by her party after she publicly endorsed Republican U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, whom she had previously endorsed and pledged to support through the general election, despite lingering tensions from their August primary. Over the past few weeks, the congresswoman has changed her position on supporting El-Sayed, moving from a position that was critical of the nominee but still supportive of the overall ticket, to outright joining Rogers at a Detroit church on Sunday where she heaped praise on Rogers for supporting some of her campaign platforms involving housing and Black-owned businesses. Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers called a ‘disgrace’ at Detroit unity roundtable Later, on CNN, Stevens said that she found El-Sayed’s campaign to be getting “angrier” against those who opposed him, and cited what she felt were instances of antisemitism from the campaign. Stevens said that ranged from campaigning with controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker to his lack of condemnation of an ad purchased by a political action committee run by Piker’s uncle. “Abdul has been getting angrier and angrier, and I was just trying to help,” Stevens told CNN. “I endorsed him, and that ad was very painful. There are so many Democrats who want to vote for the Democratic nominee, and they’re just being told this is a party you don’t belong in. This is a campaign you don’t belong in. … I’m making a decision here, and that’s just where I landed on.” Stevens could not, however, pinpoint an exact moment on when it was that she changed her mind, saying the decision had been building up for her and that Sunday’s turn to Rogers represented “a weight off her shoulders.” Before Stevens decided to support Rogers, which appeared to be a snap decision earlier Sunday morning, as she told CNN, Stevens was set to attend a church service with El-Sayed and U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina, a former Stevens supporter who was backing El-Sayed after he became the nominee. The engagement was brokered by U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Ann Arbor, who had played the intermediary between El-Sayed’s campaign and Stevens. State Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak), U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) and state Rep. Alabas Farhat (D-Dearborn) listen to speakers at a Democratic Party unity rally on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 outside of the UAW world headquarters in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)Former U.S. Rep. Andy Levin speaks at a Democratic Party unity rally on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 outside of the UAW world headquarters in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)State Rep. Stephanie Young (D-Detroit) speaks at a Democratic Party unity rally on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 outside of the UAW world headquarters in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)State Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak) speaks at a Democratic Party unity rally on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 outside of the UAW world headquarters in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance) The congresswoman had agreed but put conditions on the visit, including a call that El-Sayed disavow the ad produced by Ugyur, and other examples of rhetoric El-Sayed used to question the U.S. relationship with Israel. A major platform of El-Sayed’s campaign is acknowledging Israel has been committing a genocide in its war against Hamas in Gaza. While that determination remains controversial, it is backed up by multiple international organizations including Amnesty International, Doctors Without Borders and a United Nations commission. El-Sayed did not budge and asked Stevens’ campaign to stay out of the race through Tuesday’s election. Stevens repeatedly told CNN that being disinvited from the church event marked a turning point. It was reported that several of her staff were waiting for her at North End Church of God in Christ in Detroit, where El-Sayed and Clyburn were holding a Souls to the Polls event on Sunday. Instead, Stevens showed up at the Perfecting Union church, led by Pastor Marvin Winans of gospel music fame, to take in a morning of worship with Rogers, his wife, and Stevens’ fiance, attorney Jason Turkish. Gongwer News Service reported that former Michigan. Gov. Jim Blanchard said he had spoken to Stevens Saturday night and she said she would support El-Sayed. Blanchard told the outlet that Turkish, who had openly supported Rogers over the last few weeks, may have had a strong influence on Stevens’ decision. “He was all distraught,” Blanchard told Gongwer. “He was all strung out about Abdul. I let her know, he’s not a good influence.” Either way, the move sent shockwaves across the political universe in Michigan and beyond. Rep. Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Mike Rogers was despicable, and she must be removed from the House Democratic Caucus, @hakeemjeffries. We will double down our efforts to elect @AbdulElSayed on Tuesday. Joint statement from @IfNotNowOrg @MPowerAction & @OurRevolution: https://t.co/iWZrrCKVP4 — Yasmine Taeb (@YasmineTaeb) November 2, 2026 Several national Democrats, including those who had openly supported Stevens in the primary, said her endorsement of Rogers was a betrayal, including one of her biggest national surrogates, Neera Tanden. Supporting Mike Rogers “is a betrayal of everything Haley Stevens has fought for her entire career,” Tanden said in an X post. “It’s also a betrayal of all of her supporters that believed in her.” Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel wrote in an X post that Stevens was no longer a Democrat and she had no opportunity to run as a Democrat in the future after her stunt with Rogers. The party removed Stevens from its elected officials page entirely, taking down both her name and her photo from the list. Instead of going all in on Stevens, El-Sayed took the higher ground, called her antics a distraction, and urged members of the media to stay focused on his campaign messages rather than the drama of the race. “At the end of the day, I don’t think about Haley Stevens,” El-Sayed said. “None of this matters.” In a media scrum outside the church on Sunday afternoon, El-Sayed was adamant that he would only take questions that had to do with his campaign and its policy points and that he would end the press availability if any “horse race” questions emerged. .@AbdulElSayed calls @HaleyforMI’s maneuvering today “a distraction” from the issues in the race. “None of this matters,” he said of the distraction. “I don’t think much about Haley Stevens. https://t.co/S8vEyUpvd8 — Ben Solis (@bensolis1) November 1, 2026 Those types of questions were immediately shouted at El-Sayed, and he promptly ended the press event to begin his event with Clyburn. Clyburn praised El-Sayed without mentioning Stevens on Sunday. “We have been doing what we possibly can to make this great country of ours accessible and affordable for all of our citizens,” Clyburn said. “This campaign is about making healthcare and education accessible for all our citizens. It’s about making housing, and energy affordable for all of our citizens. And it’s about having candidates for office who will be accountable to all of our citizens.” Clyburn said he was pleased to be in Detroit with El-Sayed and to stand “in solidarity” with his campaign. Dingell, whose voice was hoarse, strained and dry by Sunday evening, was the one of several main speakers at a unity event held outside of UAW headquarters in downtown Detroit. She also urged the national media to not become distracted by what she called drama in the 11th hour of the race. “I’m just going to say it straight,” Dingell said Sunday. “There has just been too much drama created by national media and not enough attention on the people I talk to every day. If you’re worried about the direction that the country is going in, and what we have done to the African American community … Do you think that Mike Rogers, a Republican senator, will support us in doing any of that?” Other speakers included state Sen. Jeremy Moss of Bloomfield, who is running for Stevens’ 11th District seat, state Rep. Donavan McKinney of Detroit, who is running to replace U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar in the 13th District, and former U.S. Rep. Andy Levin, who was defeated by Stevens in the 2022 primary. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE State Sen. Mallory McMorrow of Royal Oak, who had been in the race for the U.S. Senate before she dropped out, also spoke about the stakes of the election and called out Stevens — without naming her — for the dustup she caused on Sunday morning. “The message that I hope you heard today is that we are locked in,” McMorrow said. “Are we ready to ignore all of the nonsense? Because let me tell you, my phone has been pretty busy today. I don’t know if you saw some news, but here’s the thing: a lot of those texts and a lot of those phone calls were not from Michiganders, they are from reporters all across the country who are treating this election like an episode of Real Housewives of Michigan.” McMorrow was adamant that this was “not a reality TV show” or about “people’s emotions” or someone trying to get “their last 15 minutes before they no longer have a title.” “This is about Michiganders, because today, while all of those messages were coming in, I heard from people in church this morning … who said what do we do to stop this president?” McMorrow said. “I want to answer all the reporters who texted me to ask, ‘is this going to change anything?’ Are we divided? No. Are we united? Yes. Are we going turn out every vote? Yes. Are we going to lock in and send Abdul El-Sayed to the Senate? Yes.”

articles.description: Michigan lawmakers introduced legislation, Senate Bill 1035 and House Bill 6092, that would modernize the state’s 2001 post-conviction DNA testing law, which advocates say creates barriers for wrongfully convicted people seeking to prove their innocence.
articles.content: George Calicut, Jr. (Dustin Hoffman, the University of Michigan Law School / Used with permission)Advocates say Michigan’s post-conviction DNA testing law established in 2001 has failed to keep pace with modern forensic science. They say for years, strict legal barriers have made it difficult for wrongfully convicted people to have DNA evidence re-tested or tested at all. Now, recently introduced bills in the state Legislature aim to update the law. They would align Michigan's rules with modern DNA testing standards.For George Calicut Jr., the current legal barriers were paralyzing.He spent 27 years in prison for the murder of a woman named Virgie Perkins; a crime he did not commit. He said he was coerced into signing a confession written by a former Detroit police detective, Barbara Simon. He said she convinced him that signing the statement would protect him from a first degree murder charge.“I had never been arrested before; didn't know what questions to ask; found myself enlisting the help of the individuals who ultimately sent me to prison," Calicut Jr. said.“She was like, 'Listen, baby, I don't want them to do that to you. You're a young Black man. I don't want to see that happen to you. You got to protect yourself.' 'Well, how do I protect myself?' 'Listen, baby, I can write a statement. It don't mean you're guilty, it just keep them from charging you with first degree murder. Let me help you.'”Simon, who is no longer with the police department, is at the center of at least six murder convictions that have been overturned or vacated due to false confessions. "Most exonerees will probably tell you that they never gave up," Calicut Jr. said. "We give up all the time. I never lost hope, but I certainly gave up.”After Simon’s misconduct was brought to light, Calicut Jr. came across a newspaper article that detailed the detective’s coercion of false confessions. He said that’s when he knew he could do something about his circumstances and came up with a plan.“They say the pen is mightier than the sword, and I had no money and I said, ‘I'm going to go to the law library and I'm going to write lawyers every week,’” Calicut explained. He said he wrote to lawyers until somebody heard him, and eventually they did.The Michigan Innocence Clinic and the Cooley Law School Innocence Project saw potential in his case and took it on.Jessa Webber, a staff attorney at the Cooley Innocence Project who represented Calicut Jr., noted that securing an exoneration through the current law is exceptionally difficult."Instead of filing for post-conviction DNA testing, the alternative is to reach out to a prosecutor's office and try to get one of those stipulations for testing," Webber said.In this case, she’s referring to a stipulation, where an attorney reaches out directly to the prosecutor's office to negotiate an agreement to test DNA evidence.Calicut's legal team took their evidence directly to the Wayne County Prosecutor’s Conviction Integrity Unit. That office agreed to conduct modern touch DNA testing on skin cells left on 27-year-old preserved physical evidence. The results pointed to an entirely different person, leading to Calicut Jr.’s exoneration.“Yeah, we're exonerated, but you always still feel like you gotta prove that you're innocent,” Calicut Jr. said.Webber said the companion bills in the state Senate and House (Senate Bill 1035 and House Bill 6092) were written specifically to dismantle these legal roadblocks. If passed, the legislation would allow a defendant to petition for DNA testing regardless of whether they were convicted following a trial or pleaded guilty, provided the evidence is available.The legislation would also scrap the state's 2001 cutoff date.Under the current law, defendants convicted after January 8, 2001, cannot ask for evidence to be re-tested unless the original results were inconclusive. But Webber said forensic science in 2001 looks nothing like science today."Now we understand that just touching a piece of evidence can be enough to deposit DNA," Webber explained. "A defendant back in the early 2000s might not have had access to DNA testing prior to trial, and then would be barred from pursuing testing under the statute because testing wasn't performed back then."The bills would also lower the legal burden of proof. Currently, defendants must present "clear and convincing" evidence just to get a judge to review their petition.“[The current statue] standard is higher than any other standard in the state,” Webber said. “We want to bring the DNA statute in line with the other post-conviction remedies available, because now it makes it really hard to get relief even if there is DNA evidence that's exculpatory, that's obtained via testing from the statute.”Additionally, the legislation would mandate that police departments preserve all biological material.Democratic State Sen. Sue Shink, a co-sponsor of the Senate bill, said updating these standards is ultimately a matter of government accountability."People need to have a chance to have all the evidence in their case considered," Shink said. "I think one of the worst things a government can do is to put somebody in prison when that person is innocent. If a mistake was made, it can be corrected, and this bill will allow that to happen."While House Bill 6092 has yet to see movement, Senate Bill 1035 was voted unanimously out of committee this fall. The Prosecuting Attorneys Association of Michigan Legislative Committee voted late last week to oppose SB 1035. A spokesperson for the group said the committee chair David Gilbert said the legislation would take away a lot of guardrails. Gilbert was not available for an interview.In the meantime, exonerees like George Calicut Jr. are left living with the aftermath of a system that took more than two decades to listen to him."I'm telling the same story today that I told 27 years ago," Calicut Jr. said. "So imagine how I feel now being out here and people telling me 'you're exonerated and you're innocent.' I have joy, but I'm not happy."

US midterms: In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed's Democratic rival backs Republican Senate candidate in stunning move
articles.content: By Nicolas Chapuis (New York (United States) correspondent) The Senate race in Michigan is already one of the most closely watched in the country, and just two days before the vote on Tuesday, November 3, it took an unexpected turn. Haley Stevens, a Democratic member of Congress who lost her party's primary to Abdul El-Sayed in August, publicly endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday. This reversal could have a major impact on this tight race, the outcome of which is critical for control of the Senate. Stevens released a video filmed in her car to announce her support for the opposing camp. "Hey Michigan, as you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for US Senate, Abdul, said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he's right, and that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today. I don't belong in Abdul's campaign." Earlier, she joined the Republican candidate at a religious service at Detroit's Perfecting Church, a Black community church in the city. This blow to the Democratic campaign capped months of mounting tension. The primary was extremely contentious between the two candidates, particularly over the situation in the Middle East. El-Sayed, 42, who would become the first Muslim to serve in the Senate if victorious on Tuesday, is staunchly pro-Palestinian, while Stevens, 43, is one of Israel's strongest supporters among Democrats in Congress. Pro-Israel advocacy groups in the US poured nearly $40 million into supporting Stevens's candidacy – or attacking El-Sayed's. It was to no avail. You have 74.23% of this article left to read. Abu Dhabi's ADNOC, G42 sign deal with OpenAI as Sam Altman travels to UAE
articles.content: DUBAI, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Abu Dhabi’s ADNOC and artificial intelligence firm G42 on Monday signed a deal with OpenAI under which the state energy firm will integrate advanced AI capabilities across its operations, the Abu Dhabi Media Office said. The deal was signed as the ChatGPT maker’s CEO Sam Altman met with Abu Dhabi’s Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Abu Dhabi and attended the United Arab Emirates’ biggest oil show, ADIPEC. US oil firms ExxonMobil and Chevron last week cancelled plans for their executives to travel to the Gulf country and join the event, citing security concerns. Fears of fresh US attacks on Iran and retaliatory strikes by Tehran have gripped the oil markets in recent days. US President Donald Trump has said he would not launch an attack on Iran before the US midterm elections on November 3, but on Friday he said Washington may carry out another military operation against Iran.
